It is therefore a duty (and a sacred duty) in such a matter, more than in any other, not to form an opinion except after the most mature examination.”—7th. It is so much in the nature of things that discoveries in the physical sciences should precede and be the occasion of progress in the intellectual ones, that, far from doing harm, this order reciprocally favors the advancement of both kinds of science. See, if not, e.g., the advantages, not merely material but moral, which progress in the means of communication brings with it, and the origin to which they must be attributed.—In former times all the sea voyages that were undertaken were very paltry and hazardous: the property of direction is discovered in the magnet, and forthwith the seaman takes heart to venture, and now seeks to launch out upon unknown seas: the passage to India by the Cape of Good Hope is accomplished, and at last, two thousand leagues away, the famous world of Columbus is discovered. How many questions are not raised in all the branches of human knowledge on the occasion of so portentous a discovery! Questions not only physical and mathematical, but theological, moral, philological, political, and all of them eminently philosophical! Without the pointing of a wretched little piece of iron toward the poles of the world, would so vast a field have been opened to human speculations? How many material advantages do not the admirable means of communication which iron and steam supply today offer to the peoples! (1) Yet these utilities are still nothing [p. 208] material in comparison with the moral advantages they bring to the human race. What a difference, or, to put it better, what a fountain of differences does the invention of printing alone not establish between ancient and modern peoples! So then, the history of man’s understanding is pointing out to us with its finger that discoveries in the physical order precede and are the occasion of advances in the moral order; or, what is the same, that the former comes first, and is consequently the easier and more perceptible. “For observing comes before deducing; receiving impressions before reflecting them: being a child before being a man: walking before explaining the gait.” I had, then, more than enough reason to affirm that “to begin with physics, or in general with the natural sciences, is to begin at the beginning; and that man naturally feels himself carried away to the contemplation of external objects by the countless sensations with which they assail all his senses.” Since the Dómine shows himself so fond of quotations, I am going to treat him to a few which, in spite of their aptness, I left in the inkwell in my former Memoir for brevity’s sake. Jouffroy speaks, and speaks as he is wont, giving us at once all the elegance of the philosophers of the ancient academy and the admirable talent for exposition that modern science demands.—“Now then, it is an undeniable fact that our attention turns far more spontaneously to exterior objects than to internal phenomena. Is this perchance a new result of habit, or in part the work of nature? Here is a question on which diverse opinions may be formed. For when we consider what a multitude of needs tend to fix the child’s attention, and to hold the man’s, upon external things, what a variety of objects social relations and the inexhaustible field of nature present to his curiosity and to his passions, we shall find ourselves obliged to confess that, even if we had no natural inclination to turn our attention [p. 209] toward external objects before internal ones, the circumstances of our condition would be sufficient to impart this bent to our intelligence; and, on the other hand, whether we are deceived by the force of habit, or whether the instinct of our intelligence naturally drags it to look outward before reflecting upon itself, it would be difficult for a sensible and impartial man to reject outright the possibility of a primitive inclination. But be this as it may, the fact that attention is in effect directed toward external objects always remains incontestable; and surely to this propensity, no less than to the paramount necessity of providing for the preservation of our existence and for the innumerable needs of our body, must we attribute the preeminence which the natural sciences have attained over the philosophical in the intellectual development of the human race.”—A truth which I could demonstrate more and more, by showing that all the theological and cosmogonic systems of the Hindus, of the Egyptians, of the Greeks, and in general of all the most notable philosophers and legislators of antiquity, are merely physical systems, founded on the observation of natural phenomena; and this I wished to let be glimpsed in my Memoir when I said that “the first investigations bore, as was natural, before all else upon natural phenomena, reminding the writer (Mr. Rumilio) in passing that Thales of Miletus, Pythagoras, and before them their masters the Egyptians, and after them the great Aristotle, began their studies with the inquiry into natural phenomena.” And see here, no doubt, one of the matters touched upon in my writing which the Dómine passes over, because he believes it, like others, of lesser importance. This gentleman has not seen that the point in question bears so directly on the principal question that it is one of the best data for elucidating it. But further on he will be shown that there is not a single particular in my Memoir that does not matter very principally to the question, since the whole [p. 210] of it is made up, rather than of long explanations, of mere indications on the most principal points;—hoping to convince him that even that part which he believes accessory is calculated to carry conviction more intimately to the minds of the readers.—And what more irrefragable proof of the necessity of saying something more still than the very doubts that still assail the mind of Mr. Dómine? On this account I cannot but earnestly beg him (for I am trying in all seriousness to satisfy his understanding), since the present writing too cannot go beyond mere indications in some parts, for just fear of becoming interminable (for this question embraces all the questions of Philosophy), to be so good as to point out to me separately each one of the points that require more elucidation, in order to impress upon him more and more the force of my proofs, which I shall take a very special pleasure in furnishing him as far as lies within my reach, although, to tell the truth, I should take more in receiving light from a master as competent as a whole Dómine must be. Let us not stray, however, from our principal subject.

(1) I do not wish to be confused for an instant with those whom I call the materialists of politics, that is to say, those who more napoleonico [in the Napoleonic manner] maintain that purely material advances suffice for the happiness and well-being of man and of societies. No one has raised his voice more strongly against so scandalous an immorality than he who writes these rough lines, and this is borne out, among other proofs, by the following proposition, which is found in a Syllabus of Philosophy published as early as 1835:—“The morality of interest opens before us an abyss of evils;” and here, among its necessary consequences, is one of those I enumerated.... “2nd. The pretension of contenting man with physical enjoyments alone”. In that same Syllabus the utilitarians are in part combated, though not with the weapons of the spiritualist philosophers, but simply with those of observation, by proving that the doctrine is not complete for want of that indispensable ingredient for compounding science.

A proof likewise of the great share which Jouffroy attributes to method in the growth of the natural sciences is found in the following passage from another of his writings: “This new spirit, he says, introduced into the natural sciences, has substituted for the reign of opinions that of observation, and has made them take more steps in half a century than they had taken since the creation of the world.” That is why Jouffroy sighs, and with him sigh all who desire true advances in the intellectual sciences (even those who, like Cousin so often, and not so much Jouffroy himself, are inconsistent with the very principles of Eclecticism), for the application of so vivifying a method to psychological investigations, the only method that can raise them to the rigor and exactness of demonstration, indispensable conditions of all science. As I have been undeceived that it availed me nothing to have quoted, in brief and

[p. 211]

> larga en mi anterior Memoria para encarecer las dificulta- des que cercaban á las ciencias intelectuales y el estado de atraso en que yacían , quiero todavía acotar dos o tres pa- sajes más de Cousin y solo el epígrafe de Verulamio , esco- gido por Kant para frontis nada menos que de su gran obra de la Razón pura ; sin perjuicio de cuanto sobre el particu-lar habré de decir á Vd . en el análisis de su párrafo siguien . te , pues aún no está siquiera terminada la lista de motivos que estoy formando para hacerle comprender porque ha de ser " más difícil conocer las propiedades de nuestro sér que las de los demás séres de la naturaleza . " Hé aquí los pasajes de Cousin , y cuenta que solo se ale- gan para demostrar que todos los filósofos sienten como por instinto y resultado de sus propios estudios , la necesi-dad , la urgencia imprescindible de apelar á la única ánco- ra de esperanza : al método de la observación . De intento me abstengo de citar autores de la escuela sensualista , pues ya se echa de ver que forzosamente han de abundar en ta-les ideas . En una Memoria sobre la clasificación de las " Cuestiones y escuelas filosóficas ", después de hacer una reseña circunstanciada sobre las condiciones de una clasifi-cación de las mencionadas       cuestiones , después de haber proclamado , como manifesté en mi primer escrito , la supe-rioridad del método experimental como el lauro de nuestro siglo , después .... (mucho recomendaría yo al Dómine la lectura de este trabajo de Cousin ) se pregunta á si mismo : " y ha habido un solo filósofo que las haya llenado hasta ahora ( aquellas condiciones )? Si tal fuera tendríamos una ciencia metafísica , como existen una geometría y una quími-ca.  Por lo menos ¿han distinguido los filósofos siquiera esas diferentes casillas ó compartimentos     del gran cuadro , ya que no han podido llenarlas ? ¿Han bosquejado por ven-tura los contornos y proporciones del edificio , ya que no han podido levantarlo ? Si tal fuera , habría una ciencia co-menzada , un camino abierto , un método ya definido ( y cui-dado que yo no voy tan allá , pues ni creo la ciencia tan

at length, in my former Memoir, in order to stress the difficulties that beset the intellectual sciences and the state of backwardness in which they lay, I wish still to set down two or three more passages of Cousin, and only the epigraph from Verulam chosen by Kant as the frontispiece of no less than his great work on Pure Reason; without prejudice to all that I shall have to say to you on the subject in the analysis of your following paragraph, for the list of reasons I am drawing up to make you understand why it should be “more difficult to know the properties of our own being than those of the other beings of nature” is not even finished yet.

Here are the passages of Cousin; and mark that they are adduced only to demonstrate that all philosophers feel, as by instinct and as the result of their own studies, the necessity, the imperative urgency, of appealing to the only anchor of hope: to the method of observation. I purposely abstain from citing authors of the sensationalist school, since it is plain to see that they must of necessity abound in such ideas. In a Memoir on the classification of “Philosophical Questions and Schools,” after giving a detailed review of the conditions for a classification of the said questions, after having proclaimed, as I showed in my first writing, the superiority of the experimental method as the laurel of our century, after.... (I would warmly recommend to the Dómine the reading of this work of Cousin’s) he asks himself: “And has there been a single philosopher who has fulfilled them up to now (those conditions)? If so, we should have a metaphysical science, as there exist a geometry and a chemistry. Have the philosophers at least distinguished those different pigeonholes or compartments of the great table, since they have not been able to fill them? Have they perchance sketched the outlines and proportions of the edifice, since they have not been able to raise it? If so, there would be a science begun, a road opened, a method already defined (and mark you, I do not go so far, for I neither believe science so

[p. 212]

> atrasada ni estoy aquí de mantenedor de las opiniones de Cousín : se trata de un hecho , el atraso de las ciencias in-telectuales y la necesidad de aplicarles el método experi-mental .) Pero si los filósofos no han sabido ni llenar esas casillas del cuadro filosófico , ni siquiera percibirlas y dis-tinguirlas ¿qué es lo que han hecho ? Helo aquí en breves palabras . " Los primeros filósofos todo lo han tratado y todo resuel-to , pero confusamente ; todo lo han tratado , pero sus méto-dos son arbitrarios y artificiales .....     Descartes mismo , á pesar de todo el vigor de su entendimiento , no penetró todo el alcance de la distinción entre el sujeto y el objeto ... no le hizo fuerza como debía el abismo que separa al su jeto del objeto ; y después de haber planteado bien el pro-blema , este grande hombre lo resolvió con demasiada lige-reza ." Aquí vendría perfectamente hablar de lo que hizo el gran Leibnitz ; pero ya me voy cansando á mí mismo y cansando sin duda á los lectores con tanta cita , y hay toda-vía muchas por hacer en otra parte del presente ómás bien del futuro escrito , pues ya es menester ir dando pun-to para este correo , aun antes de concluir la enumeración de los porquées en que nos hallamos , que ya le robamos más de media docena de columnas al Diario de mañana ; y sien--to á fé mía , echarle aquí el siste á la pluma , pues en la prime-ra parada salí mejor librado que en la presente , en la cual ni siquiera me ha sido posible cerrar con un punto , como me aconteció en la primera : pero paciencia , que en reuniendo todos los Diarios que contengan las partes , resultará sin re-medio el todo , y ya estaremos del otro lado . Entre tanto, y paciencia por otra vez , allá vá el texto prometido de Ve-rulamio , que sirve de portada á la obra magna del filósofo de Konigsberga , y que yo de muy buen talante lo estampa-ría al frente y fin como alma y cuerpo de las presentes y futuras discusiones que con otros y entre nosotros medien . " De nobis ipsis silemus : de re autem quæ      agitur , petimus : ut homines eam non opinionem , sed opus        esse cogitent : ac

backward, nor am I here as champion of the opinions of Cousin: it is a question of a fact, the backwardness of the intellectual sciences and the necessity of applying the experimental method to them.) But if philosophers have known neither how to fill those pigeonholes of the philosophical table, nor even how to perceive and distinguish them, what is it that they have done? Here it is in a few words.

“The first philosophers have treated everything and resolved everything, but confusedly; they have treated everything, but their methods are arbitrary and artificial......... Descartes himself, in spite of all the vigor of his understanding, did not penetrate the whole bearing of the distinction between the subject and the object... the abyss that separates the subject from the object did not strike him as it ought; and after having stated the problem well, this great man resolved it with too much lightness.” Here it would be perfectly in place to speak of what the great Leibnitz did; but I am already beginning to tire myself, and no doubt the readers as well, with so many quotations, and there are still many to be made in another part of the present, or rather of the future, writing; for it is now necessary to begin bringing things to a stop for this mail, even before concluding the enumeration of the whys in which we are engaged, since we are already robbing tomorrow’s Diario of more than half a dozen columns; and upon my faith I am sorry to cry halt to my pen here, for at the first stage I came off better than at the present one, in which it has not even been possible for me to close with a full stop, as I managed in the first: but patience, for once all the Diarios containing the parts are gathered together, the whole will needs result, and we shall be on the other side. Meanwhile, and patience once more, here goes the promised text of Verulam, which serves as title-page to the great work of the philosopher of Königsberg, and which I would most willingly print at the head and at the end, as the soul and body of the present and future discussions that may pass with others and among ourselves. “De nobis ipsis silemus: de re autem quæ agitur, petimus: ut homines eam non opinionem, sed opus esse cogitent: ac [Of ourselves we say nothing: but on behalf of the matter in hand we ask that men think it not an opinion but a work; and

[p. 213]

> pro certo habeant , non sectae nos alicujis , aut placiti , sed -                           -utilitatis et amplitudinis humanæ fundamenta moliri . Dein-de ut suis commodis æqui in commune consulant et ipsi in partem veniant . Praeterea ut bene sperent neque ins-taurationem nostram ut quiddam infinitum et ultra morta- -lefingant , et animo concipiant ; quum revera sit infiniti erro-ris finis et terminus legítimus . " Resulta pues que en con-cepto de los más grandes metafisicos las ciencias intelec-tuales son en resumidas cuentas un mero y simple postula-do ó desideratum : algo más de lo que necesitaba yo para afirmar que estaban en mantillas respecto de las naturales : verdad que irá apareciendo más y más refulgente con el curso de esta discusión ; al punto de penetrar su resplandor hasta por los mismos ojos que quieran cerrarse á este rio de luz concentrada en un mismo foco , y derramada sobre un mismo punto .

pro certo habeant, non sectae nos alicujus, aut placiti, sed utilitatis et amplitudinis humanæ fundamenta moliri. Deinde ut suis commodis æqui—in commune consulant—et ipsi in partem veniant. Praeterea ut bene sperent neque instaurationem nostram ut quiddam infinitum et ultra mortale fingant, et animo concipiant; quum revera sit infiniti erroris finis et terminus legitimus.” [hold it for certain that we are laying the foundations not of any sect or doctrine, but of human utility and greatness. Next, that, fair to their own interests, they take counsel for the common good, and themselves come in for a share. Further, that they be of good hope, and not imagine and conceive our Instauration as something infinite and beyond what is mortal; since in truth it is the end and lawful limit of infinite error.]—It follows, then, that in the judgment of the greatest metaphysicians the intellectual sciences are, when all is said and done, a mere and simple postulate or desideratum: something more than I needed in order to affirm that they were in swaddling clothes compared with the natural sciences: a truth which will go on appearing more and more resplendent as this discussion proceeds; to the point that its brightness will penetrate even through the very eyes that would close themselves against this river of light concentrated in one focus, and poured out upon one single point.

[p. 214]

> IV. DUPLICA A LA REPLICA         DEL "DOMINE ,” inserta en la Gaceta de Puerto Príncipe de 17 de Noviembre   último ( 1).. "Pro me laboras ." (Continúa ) He ocupado ya diez columnas de los Diarios anteriores , sin haber salido todavía de la primera de mi antagonista , cuyo artículo abraza mas de tres en la Gaceta de Puerto Príncipe ; y así por este motivo como por haberle repetida-mente indicado mi disposición á entrar en pormenores , y cuando guste , sobre todos aquellos puntos que por la brevedad con que estén tratados , requieran elucidación , me será lícito continuar el camino á paso mas acelerado . 8 °-También las lenguas necesita conocer el que desée penetrar á fondo los fenómenos del entendimiento . Y digo las lenguas , por que no basta el conocimiento de una sola para suministrar los datos que ha menester la gramática general . Las lenguas son el primer monumento para la historia del espíritu humano : así pues , contrayéndonos  al punto que nos ocupa , es de recomendarse su estudio , y ha de preceder al de la Lógica , no tanto á causa de la impor-tancia de la expresión de las ideas , ( que es en sí una gran carta de recomendación ) cuanto por ofrecerse en los idio-mas el fiel reflejo de las operaciones del entendimiento , y la historia mas exacta y completa de su desarrollo . Así , la lengua de un pueblo acusa lo que es , lo que ha sido y como ha sido este mismo pueblo . Las lenguas en fin nos presen-tan las mejores pruebas de careo ó confronta que imagi- -narse pueden para esperimentar y acrisolar las doctrinas mas importantes de la ciencia de las ideas . He ahí pues otro elemento que dificulta el problema , convenciéndonos (1 )   Diario de la Habana de 6 de Enero de 1839.   ( A. Ζ .)

IV.

## Rejoinder to the Reply of the “Dómine,”

printed in the Gaceta de Puerto Príncipe of November 17 last (1).

## “Pro me laboras.”

[You labor for me.]

(Continued)

I have already taken up ten columns of the preceding issues of the Diario without yet having got beyond the first column of my antagonist, whose article covers more than three in the Gaceta de Puerto Príncipe; and so, for this reason as well as for having repeatedly indicated to him my readiness to enter into particulars, whenever he pleases, on all those points which, from the brevity with which they are treated, may require elucidation, I shall be permitted to continue on my way at a quicker pace.

8º—Languages, too, must be known by whoever wishes to penetrate to the bottom of the phenomena of the understanding. And I say languages, because the knowledge of a single one is not enough to furnish the data that general grammar requires. Languages are the first monument for the history of the human mind: and so, confining ourselves to the point that occupies us, their study is to be recommended, and must precede that of Logic, not so much on account of the importance of the expression of ideas (which is in itself a great letter of recommendation) as because in languages there is offered the faithful reflection of the operations of the understanding, and the most exact and complete history of its development. Thus the language of a people declares what that people is, what it has been, and how it has been. Languages, in short, present us with the best proofs of cross-examination or confrontation that can be imagined for testing and refining the most important doctrines of the science of ideas.— Here, then, is another element that complicates the problem, convincing us

(1) Diario de la Habana of January 6, 1839. (A. Z.)

[p. 215]

> de la necesidad de su precedencia al estudio de la Lógica propiamente tal , en el supuesto de estar convenido con el Dómine que por Lógica se entiende la "ciencia que tiene por objeto exponer los fenómenos y teoría de la inteligencia ." Yo no tendría mas que ir sacando consecuencias de esta de finición para pulverizar cuanto ha sentado el Dómine en su papel . ¿Se ha puesto este señor á refléxionar por un instan- -te cuánto abraza aquella definición ? " ¡ Todos " los fenóme-nos de la inteligencia ! y luego   ......  la teoría de la inteli-gencia ! ¿Dónde están los fenómenos de la inteligencia ? Escondidos en la conciencia , y es menester desentrañarlos ; complicados con los de la sensibilidad , y es menester des-lindarlos ; modificados por la edad , el sexo , el temperamen -to , el clima , la educación , el estado de salud y enfermedad , y es menester tomar cuenta de tantas causas modificado-ras ; confundidos à veces con los del instinto , y es menester distinguirlos ; oscurecidos por el hábito , y es menester . aclararlos ; reflejados en las lenguas , y es menester recibir su luz ; envueltos á veces en los sistemas , y es menester -sacarlos en claro ; derramados por todo el ámbito de las -ciencias , y es menester recogerlos y clasificarlos . De aquí 9.    La necesidad de familiarizarse con el conocimiento de los sistemas filosóficos : otro inconveniente para la resolu-ción del problema , otra piedra de toque para las doctrinas ; -y esto es ya internarse en el vasto campo de la historia -de la filosofía . 10 . De aquí también como paso prévio , como conditio sine qua non el recoger los datos de las otras ciencias como hechos ó ejemplos para la ciencia de las ideas , para la teoría de las teorías . Esto es tan óbvio , que no podemos entablar discusión alguna sobre tales materias sin contraernos inmediatamente á la naturaleza de las ciencias físicas , matemáticas ó morales : ni puede ser de otra manera .   ¿Cómo hubiéramos podido al principio de este papel , ventilar la cuestión de los signos sin algunas nocio-nes algebraicas ? ¿Cómo era posible haber esplicado la causa del rigor y precisión de semejantes signos , y su superioridad [p. 216] sobre los de las lenguas vulgares , sin habernos infor- mado primero de todo el artificio del método algebráico ? - ¿Y no sacamos de este análisis un documento precioso para la ciencia de las ideas ? Abranse los libros de todos los psi- cologistas y metafísicos modernos , y desde los mismos um- brales se tropezará con las nociones tomadas de las otras ciencias , como base fundamental , como conocimientos pre- viamente adquiridos ; y no sólo se encontrará á las cien- cias naturales y matemáticas ofreciendo la hueste pa- ra la campaña (los hechos ) sino sirviendo de caudillo y modelo para dirigir y marchar en la acción ( su método ) ¿ Quiere V. que le acote en comprobación á todos los meta- - físicos modernos de todas las escuelas , desde Cartesio has ta nuestros días ? De nada me valieron tantas citas como amontoné en mi anterior trabajo y qué remedio ?-Volver á citar :  pero sólo lo haré con Kant y Cousin          - que ya tiene V. otra cita al mismo propósito de Jouffroy ; y si las quiere todas no hay mas que avisar y quedará servido , á pesar del fastidio que trae consigo la ingrata tarea de co- piar . Todo el prólogo á la segunda edición de la " Crítica de la razón pura, " ó mejor dicho , la obra entera podría estrac- tarse en comprobación , pues toda ella es una continua dis- cusión sobre la nuturaleza de las verdades de cada ciencia y los métodos adoptados en ella . Antes de fundar cosa al- trazar el plano de la obra , ocupar el terreno antes de levantar el edificio , discutir antes de enseñar . Tal es el procedimien- to de Kant . Elegiré , pues , tan sólo las palabras siguien tes como las mas adecuadas á nuestro propósito : " En esa tentativa de cambiar la marcha que hasta ahora ha seguido la metafisica , proponiéndonos por modelo á los geómetras y fisicos para lograr en ella una total revolución , se cifra pues el objeto de esta crítica de la razón puramente espe- culativa . Ella es un tratado del método , no un sistema de la ciencia misma ( parecen mandadas decir las palabras pa- ra la cuestión ) ; pero en medio de eso ella demarca toda su *   guna era indispensable recoger y escoger los materiales y [p. 217] -esfera , así respecto á sus límites como á toda su estructura . interna . " No es menester copiar más de Kant Agreguemos las espresiones de Cousin en el apéndice á sus fragmentos ." 'Esclusivamente ocupado ( refiere sus tareas en la escuela normal ) en introducir en la metafísica el método de las cien-cias naturales , yo no traspasaba los límites de la psicología ; y hoy mismo estoy bien léjos de arrepentirme de esta circunspección ; pues ante todo , se debe fecundar el enten-dimiento , y lo que lo fecunda es el método . Con el método no se fundan sectas , empero se puede comunicar un movi-miento útil ." 11. Dije en mi Memoria que el capítulo de la enagena-ción mental por sí solo es un episodio que respecto de los conocimientos auxiliares que requiere , se vuelve otro asun-to principal en el estudio del hombre : teniendo por escusa-do advertir     que procedemos bajo el concepto      de que es materia fundamental para la Psicología , la Ética y la Legis-lación . Sin salir de la Psicología , ¡ cuántos fenómenos admi-rables y dignos de ser observados para el estudio de las funciones intelectuales , no nos ofrece su perversión por todos los grados y matices con que se presenta desde el delirio de la fiebre hasta la desesperación de la manía ! ¡ Cuántas   funciones alteradas unas , y estimuladas otras al lado de algunas todavía normales en medio del desorden de las demás ! Y pasando de aquí á la moral y á la legisla-ción, cuántos datos preciosos para trazar con tino la sutil raya divisoria entre la enfermedad y el delito ! ¡Cuántas indicaciones delicadas para determinar los grados de la culpabilidad ó fragilidad de nuestra especie ! ¡ Qué estudio tan -digno , tan importante ! el más propio de todos los estudios para el linaje humano  .  el hombre . ¿Y se puede conocer al hombre sin internarse profundamente en el examen de es- tos fenómenos ? ¿Y debe ó no debe preceder este estudio al de la Lógica propiamente tal ? ¿Y no supone además se-mejante estudio el de otras ciencias naturales , como indis-pensables preliminares ? ¿Puede haber Psicología sin Fisio

of the necessity of its preceding the study of Logic properly so called, on the supposition, agreed with the Dómine, that by Logic is understood the “science whose object is to set forth the phenomena and theory of the intelligence.” I should have nothing more to do than go on drawing consequences from this definition in order to pulverize all that the Dómine has laid down in his paper. Has this gentleman stopped for an instant to reflect how much that definition embraces?—“All” the phenomena of the intelligence! and then...... the theory of the intelligence! Where are the phenomena of the intelligence? Hidden in consciousness, and they must be disentangled; complicated with those of sensibility, and they must be marked off; modified by age, sex, temperament, climate, education, the state of health and of sickness, and account must be taken of so many modifying causes; confused at times with those of instinct, and they must be distinguished; obscured by habit, and they must be cleared up; reflected in languages, and their light must be received; wrapped up at times in systems, and they must be brought out clear; scattered over the whole compass of the sciences, and they must be gathered up and classified.—Hence 9º— The necessity of becoming familiar with the knowledge of philosophical systems: another obstacle to the solution of the problem, another touchstone for doctrines;—and this is already to enter the vast field of the history of philosophy.—10º Hence, too, as a preliminary step, as a conditio sine qua non, the gathering of the data of the other sciences as facts or examples for the science of ideas, for the theory of theories. This is so obvious that we cannot open any discussion on such matters without immediately confining ourselves to the nature of the physical, mathematical or moral sciences: nor can it be otherwise. How could we, at the beginning of this paper, have aired the question of signs without some algebraic notions? How was it possible to have explained the cause of the rigor and precision of such signs, and their superiority [p. 216] over those of the vulgar tongues, without having first informed ourselves of the whole contrivance of the algebraic method? And do we not draw from this analysis a precious document for the science of ideas?—Open the books of all the modern psychologists and metaphysicians, and from the very threshold one will stumble upon notions taken from the other sciences, as a fundamental basis, as knowledge previously acquired; and one will find the natural and mathematical sciences not only furnishing the host for the campaign (the facts) but serving as captain and model for directing it and marching into action (their method)—Would you have me cite in proof all the modern metaphysicians of all the schools, from Descartes down to our own day? So many quotations as I heaped up in my previous work availed me nothing, and what remedy is there?—To quote again:—but I shall do so only with Kant and Cousin—for you already have another quotation from Jouffroy to the same purpose; and if you want them all, you have only to say the word and you shall be served, in spite of the tedium that the thankless task of copying brings with it. The whole preface to the second edition of the “Critique of Pure Reason,” or rather the entire work, might be extracted in proof, for the whole of it is one continual discussion of the nature of the truths of each science and of the methods adopted in it. Before founding anything at all it was indispensable to gather and select the materials and trace the plan of the work, to occupy the ground before raising the edifice, to discuss before teaching. Such is Kant’s procedure. I shall choose, then, only the following words, as the most suited to our purpose: “In this attempt to change the course hitherto followed by metaphysics, taking the geometers and physicists as our model so as to bring about in it a complete revolution, lies, then, the object of this critique of purely speculative reason. It is a treatise on method, not a system of the science itself (the words seem made to order for the question); but for all that it marks out its whole [p. 217] sphere, both as regards its limits and as regards its whole internal structure.” There is no need to copy more from Kant.—Let us add the expressions of Cousin in the appendix to his fragments: “Occupied exclusively (he is relating his labors at the Normal School) with introducing into metaphysics the method of the natural sciences, I did not overstep the limits of psychology; and even today I am very far from repenting of this circumspection; for before all else one must fertilize the understanding, and what fertilizes it is method. With method one does not found sects, but one can impart a useful movement.”

11º I said in my Memoir that the chapter on mental alienation is by itself an episode which, in respect of the auxiliary knowledge it requires, turns into another principal subject in the study of man: holding it needless to point out that we proceed on the understanding that it is a fundamental matter for Psychology, Ethics and Legislation. Without leaving Psychology, how many admirable phenomena, worthy of being observed for the study of the intellectual functions, does not their perversion offer us, through all the degrees and shades in which it presents itself, from the delirium of fever to the despair of mania! How many functions, some altered and others stimulated, alongside some still normal amid the disorder of the rest! And passing from here to morality and legislation, how many precious data for drawing with tact the subtle dividing line between disease and crime! How many delicate indications for determining the degrees of culpability or frailty of our species! What a worthy, what an important study! the most proper of all studies for mankind.—man. And can man be known without going deeply into the examination of these phenomena? And must this study, or must it not, precede that of Logic properly so called? And does not such a study presuppose besides that of other natural sciences, as indispensable preliminaries? Can there be Psychology without Physiology

[p. 218]

> logía , ni Fisiología , sin Física ? ¿ Qué digo sin Física ? Hoy menos que nunca , particularmente después de los experi-mentos y doctrinas de Magendie , que tienden á probar que una gran parte del atraso de la ciencia Fisiológica era de-bido á la falta de aplicación de la Física á los mismos fenó-menos vitales , muchos de los cuales no son más que los propios fenómenos de la materia inerte observados en la viviente : ¡ tan cierto es que cuanto más adelantan las cien-cias , tanto más se ensancha el horizonte de la generaliza-ción , y tanto más , por consecuencia forzosa se simplifica y despeja el vasto campo de los hechos , quedando reducidos los que al parecer eran más lejanos é inconexos á un víncu-lo universal que á todos los junta y fraterniza ! No sin har-ta razón decía el insigne Davy que la complicación es el patrimonio de los primeros albores de la ciencia . Si á este propósito me fuera concedido detenerme , yo señalaría de buen grado los errores á que han sido arrastrados los ta-lentos más esclarecidos en todos los ramos de la ciencia del hombre , sólo por falta de observación sobre su propia naturaleza . Así , por falta de fisiología , han delirado infini-tos psicologistas ; por falta de fisiología se extravió Montes-quieu y erró Helvecio : por falta de fisiología se ha desca-rriado Bentham , que tanto suele acertar ; por falta de fisio-logía se han malogrado los mejores planes de educación y los mejores educandos ; por falta de fisiología    .... Pero he pronunciado  la palabra educación , y al mágico influjo que sobre mi alma ejerce , no puedo menos que recordar el cla-mor que de todas partes se levanta en la culta Europa pa-ra hacer sentir á los institutores no solo la necesidad en que están de enseñar esta ciencia en sus establecimientos , sino la más urgente de practicar los preciosos documentos que ofrece para no malograr el precioso fruto de sus afanes : y este clamor   ha hallado eco aquende de los mares , en esa tierra clásica de la primaria educación , la república norte-americana . De aquí también otro clamor no menos univer-sal de combinar el trabajo manual con el mentul , ó sea el [p. 219] mejor  sistema de gimnástica é higiene con arreglo á los datos  que    de sí arroja la ciencia del hombre . Clamor arrancado por los innumerables hechos que ofrecen las en-fermedades y dolencias especiales de los que se consagran al estudio , en términos de socavar el edificio de su salud , ó dejarlo para siempre frágil y vacilante . Cuanto más profundicemos en la materia , tanto más nos convenceremos de la imposibilidad de dar pasos acertados en ningún ramo de cuantos dicen relación al hombre y la sociedad sin el estudio previo del hombre mismo , que ya presupone el general de la naturaleza con un sin número de especialidades . En psicología , educación , moral y legisla-ción , ya hemos amontonado algunos datos para juzgar de la imprescindible necesidad del estudio del hombre para semejantes ramos del saber humano . Respecto de la his toria , baste decir que no es dable formar juicio de innume-rables hechos sin haber formado para ello nuestro      criterio por el tipo de la naturaleza .-¿Cómo podrá graduar nuestro entendimiento los límites de lo posible y lo probable , de lo creible é increible , sin haber observado las fuerzas de la na-turaleza , ó sin guiarse por las analogías dėducidas de estas mismas observaciones , cuando le faltan nuevos esperimen-tos indispensables para fallar? "¿Pues que cosa hay que no sea milagro la primera vez que se observa ? ¡ Cuántas y cuantas no se tienen por impracticables hasta no verse que están hechas ! A cada paso dudaríamos del poderío y ma-gestad de la naturaleza de las cosas , si mirásemos sus par-tes aisladamente y no abrazásemos su totalidad con nuestro espíritu . " Asi se esplica Plinio el naturalista . La primera vez que un hombre vulgar oye decir que llueven piedras , no vacila en relegar semejante especie al país de los imposi-bles y las quimeras . ¿Y por qué ? Porque no habiendo es-tudiado la naturaleza , carece de medios y contrapesos para graduar su poder . Pero sin ir á parar hasta el rústico : aun los mismos eruditos , que suelen ( y antes más que ahora ) no abundar en conocimientos naturales , se atrevieron á tratar

, or Physiology without Physics? What am I saying, without Physics? Today less than ever, particularly after the experiments and doctrines of Magendie, which tend to prove that a great part of the backwardness of physiological science was due to the failure to apply Physics to the vital phenomena themselves, many of which are no more than the very phenomena of inert matter observed in living matter: so true is it that the further the sciences advance, the wider grows the horizon of generalization, and the more, by necessary consequence, is the vast field of facts simplified and cleared, those that seemed most remote and unconnected being reduced to a universal bond that joins them all and makes brothers of them! Not without good reason did the illustrious Davy say that complication is the patrimony of the first dawn of science. If I were permitted to dwell on this point, I would gladly point out the errors into which the most enlightened talents in all branches of the science of man have been drawn, solely for lack of observation of their own nature.—Thus, for lack of physiology, countless psychologists have raved; for lack of physiology Montesquieu went astray and Helvétius erred: for lack of physiology Bentham, who is so often right, has strayed from the path; for lack of physiology the best plans of education and the best pupils have come to nothing; for lack of physiology.... But I have pronounced the word education, and under the magic influence it exerts upon my soul, I cannot but recall the clamor that rises on every side in cultivated Europe to make teachers feel not only the necessity they are under of teaching this science in their establishments, but the still more urgent one of putting into practice the precious lessons it offers, so as not to waste the precious fruit of their toils: and this clamor has found an echo on this side of the seas, in that classic land of primary education, the North American republic. Hence, too, another clamor no less universal for combining manual labor with mental, or rather, the [p. 219] best system of gymnastics and hygiene in accordance with the data that the science of man yields of itself. A clamor wrung from the innumerable facts presented by the diseases and ailments peculiar to those who devote themselves to study, to the point of undermining the edifice of their health, or leaving it forever frail and tottering.

The more deeply we go into the matter, the more we shall be convinced of the impossibility of taking sure steps in any branch of all those that relate to man and society without the previous study of man himself, which already presupposes the general study of nature together with a countless number of specialties. In psychology, education, morality and legislation we have already heaped up some data for judging the indispensable necessity of the study of man for such branches of human knowledge. As regards history, suffice it to say that it is not possible to form a judgment on innumerable facts without having first formed our criterion for it on the pattern of nature.—How shall our understanding gauge the limits of the possible and the probable, of the credible and the incredible, without having observed the forces of nature, or without being guided by the analogies deduced from these same observations, when it lacks the new experiments indispensable for pronouncing judgment? “For what thing is there that is not a miracle the first time it is observed? How many, many things are held impracticable until they are seen done! At every step we should doubt the power and majesty of the nature of things, if we looked at its parts in isolation and did not embrace its totality with our mind.” So speaks Pliny the naturalist. The first time a common man hears it said that stones rain down, he does not hesitate to banish such a notion to the land of impossibilities and chimeras. And why? Because, not having studied nature, he lacks the means and counterweights for gauging its power. But without going so far as the rustic: even the learned themselves, who are apt (and formerly more than now) to be none too rich in natural knowledge, dared to treat

[p. 220]

> de fábula el fénómeno de los aerólitos consignado en mu-chos historiadores de la antigüedad y señaladamente en el citado Plinio . Otra cosa habría sido con entendimientos adoctrinados por la observación , pues aun caso de no ha-ber llegado á su noticia semejante hecho prodigioso , la constante esperiencia de otros portentos notados en el vas-to campo de la naturaleza , los hace forzosamente más cau-tos , circunspectos y mesurados para decidir , y por una con-secuencia indispensable , sólidos y profundos en cuantas materias traten de examinar , ó lo que es lo mismo , y hace más á nuestro propósito , ménos sujetos á errores y retroce-sos , que tantos perjuicios irrogan á la ciencia , y ménos fá-ciles de contentar con un barniz superficial , por más des-lumbrador que sea para los ojos bisoños de la muchedum-bre . Y no haya miedo que el espiritu de rigor y exactitud que reclama la ciencia esterilice ni siquiera un filon del venero inagotable del arte y de la poesía , antes fomentados que menguados con los descubrimientos de la ciencia mo-derna , como contra el dictamen de algunos literatos del día , sería harto fácil demostrarlo . No es menos irrazonable la guerra en que se trata de poner á la ciencia con la poesía , que el divorcio que se ha procurado establecer entre aque-lla misma y la religión santa de la hija de Sión . La viva impresión de las maravillas de la naturaleza , nos ha de arrebatar forzosamente á las regiones sublimes de la poe-sía . Los objetos y resortes de ésta podrán variar con ei tiempo y las circunstancias , pero su raíz está hondamente afirmada en el corazón del hombre para que pueda jamás arrancarse . La ciencia léjos de conmover esta raíz , le ofrecerá nuevos jugos , y fecundante riego . Será la poesía del siglo XIX : tendrá al mismo tiempo un vínculo común con las demás , y un carácter peculiar que la distinga . Lo que hará el estudio de las ciencias es poner cada cosa en su lugar : sus progresos impedirán que á la humanidad adulta se la pueda arrullar con el mismo instrumento , ó con el mismo tono que á la humanidad infantil : sucederá á la

as a fable the phenomenon of aerolites recorded in many historians of antiquity, and notably in the Pliny already cited. It would have been another matter with understandings schooled by observation, for even in case such a prodigious fact had not come to their notice, the constant experience of other wonders remarked in the vast field of nature makes them perforce more cautious, circumspect and measured in deciding, and, by an inevitable consequence, solid and profound in whatever matters they undertake to examine, or, what is the same thing and more to our purpose, less subject to errors and backslidings, which do so much harm to science, and less easily contented with a superficial varnish, however dazzling it may be to the raw eyes of the multitude. And let there be no fear that the spirit of rigor and exactness which science demands will sterilize so much as a single vein of the inexhaustible lode of art and poetry, which are rather fostered than diminished by the discoveries of modern science, as it would be easy enough to demonstrate against the opinion of some men of letters of the day. No less unreasonable is the war in which they try to set science against poetry than the divorce that has been sought to establish between that same science and the holy religion of the daughter of Zion. The vivid impression of the marvels of nature must perforce carry us away to the sublime regions of poetry. Its objects and springs may vary with time and circumstances, but its root is too deeply fixed in the heart of man ever to be torn out. Science, far from shaking this root, will offer it new sap and fertilizing water.— It will be the poetry of the 19th century: it will have at once a common bond with the others, and a peculiar character that distinguishes it.

What the study of the sciences will do is put each thing in its place: their progress will prevent adult humanity from being lulled with the same instrument, or in the same tone, as infant humanity: it will happen to the

[p. 221]

> especie lo mismo que sucede siempre al indivíduo : no se le distrae ya hombre con aquel mismo juguete por el que se desatinaba en la cuna , pero siempre habrá un medio de recrearle y morigerarle . ¡ Que nuevas formas no ha tomado el arte , cuando ya se creían agotadas sus fuentes , en manos de los Goethe , los Schiller , los Scott , los Byron , los Manzoni , los Lamartine y --los Hugo ! Pero qué digo nuevas formas ! nuevos asuntos nunca tratados , y que tanto caracterizan la época en que vivimos han sido admirablemente manejados por esos pre-claros ingenios ; y como para desengañarnos de que no sólo se podía cautivar el corazón con la mágia de la edad me-dia , se presenta el autor de Roma subterránea no invocan-do más númen que lo presente , y alcanzando un triunfo igual , sino superior por su noble fin , á los obtenidos por el prestigio encantador de las antiguas tradiciones .—No haya miedo pues de que en medio de los grandes descubrimien-tos que se suceden y de los grandes intereses que nos agi . tan, enmudezca un instante la musa de la humanidad . En Economía pública , ¿puede darse un paso sin esponerse á tropezar , como no se consulten los métodos y procedi- mientos de las ciencias y artes mecánicas , que constituyen una gran parte de los materiales sobre que han de recaer los razonamientos ? Véanse sino las lecciones que aún á la práctica   y sesuda Inglaterra , la nación   práctica   por exce-lencia , le da uno de sus hijos más distinguidos , el físico-matemático Cárlos Babbage , digno sucesor de Issac New-ton en la cátedra de Cambridge : lecciones consignadas en la obra titulada Economía de las manufacturas . Nadie se esperaría á primera vista que bajo tan modesta portada se incluyesen las más graves cuestiones de la Economía pú-blica ; y sin embargo tan magistralmente y bajo tan nuevos aspectos se examinan estas materias , haciendo ver la tras-cendencia de los errores que se han cometido y pueden co-meterse legislando acerca de ellos sin el previo conocimien-to de esos datos á primera vista puramente mecánicos , que

species just as it always happens to the individual: the grown man is no longer amused with the same toy he was wild about in the cradle, but there will always be a means of recreating him and tempering his manners.

What new forms has art not taken, when its springs were already thought exhausted, in the hands of the Goethes, the Schillers, the Scotts, the Byrons, the Manzonis, the Lamartines and the Hugos!— But what am I saying, new forms! new subjects never treated before, and which so characterize the age in which we live, have been admirably handled by those illustrious geniuses; and as if to undeceive us that it was not only with the magic of the Middle Ages that the heart could be captivated, the author of Roma subterránea comes forward invoking no other muse than the present, and winning a triumph equal—nay, superior by its noble end—to those obtained by the enchanting prestige of ancient traditions.—Let there be no fear, then, that amid the great discoveries that follow one upon another and the great interests that stir us, the muse of humanity will fall silent for a single instant.

In Public Economy, can a step be taken without running the risk of stumbling, unless one consults the methods and procedures of the sciences and the mechanical arts, which make up a great part of the materials on which its reasonings must bear? See, if not, the lessons which even practical and judicious England, the practical nation par excellence, receives from one of her most distinguished sons, the physicist and mathematician Charles Babbage, worthy successor of Isaac Newton in the chair at Cambridge: lessons set down in the work entitled On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures. No one would expect at first sight that under so modest a title-page the gravest questions of Public Economy should be included; and yet these matters are examined so masterfully and under such new aspects, showing the far-reaching consequences of the errors that have been and may be committed by legislating about them without previous knowledge of those data, at first sight purely mechanical, that

[p. 222]

> no queda más recurso á los economistas y legisladores que ir á aprender fisica y matemáticamente la ciencia sublime de la Economía pública en los severos libros de la Dinámi-ca y en los humildes talleres de las artes . Tan penetrado parece haber estado de idénticos principios , el traductor español de esta preciosa obra , cuanto la ha engrandecido con el título de Principios de Economía política , con que no le ocurrió bautizarla á su modesto autor . Pero donde se echó el resto á los desengaños para los legisladores y gobernantes , y en general para cuantos se ocupan de la causa pública es en la famosa obra del médico Parent -du - Chatelet , sobre la " Prostitución en la ciudad de París ," que por vía de nota cité en mi Memoria como un modelo de investigación . Vengan los jurisconsultos , los moralistas , y en general todos los que cultivan las ciencias especulativas , á iniciarse en infinitos datos que para ellos se-rán otros tantos arcanos : vengan á aprender no solo cosas , sino método para examinar y descubrir otras cosas : el mé-todo de la observación , el rigurosamente analítico , el único que merece el nombre de científico , espíritu que no se ad-quiere sino en el cultivo de las ciencias naturales y de sus inseparables cooperadoras las matemáticas . Allí verán la mejor aplicación que jamás se ha hecho de los procedi-mientos estadísticos , ó rigurosamente numéricos : esta es la lógica que reclama el siglo en que vivimos , este es el pasto que se debe suministrar á los que meditan sobre la suerte de la humanidad , y sobre los medios más eficaces de curar las dolencias morales que la aflijen . Porque el libro de Mr. Parent no como quiera es un libro eminentemente moral , sino que desde la primera hasta la postrera página abona á su autor como el más celoso abogado de las buenas costumbres , como un alma purísima , é incontaminada , á pesar de los hálitos infectos que el desempeño concienzudo de su gravísima misión le forzó á respirar ocasionalmente en el largo período de ocho años . Bien podía haber pues-to este profundo filósofo , este predicador de salud fisica y

no other recourse is left to economists and legislators than to go and learn, physically and mathematically, the sublime science of Public Economy in the severe books of Dynamics and in the humble workshops of the arts. So deeply does the Spanish translator of this precious work appear to have been imbued with these same principles, that he has magnified it with the title of Principios de Economía política, a name with which it never occurred to its modest author to christen it.

But where the last word was said in the way of disenchantments for legislators and rulers, and in general for all who concern themselves with the public cause, is in the famous work of the physician Parent-du- Châtelet, on “Prostitution in the City of Paris,” which I cited by way of a note in my Memoir as a model of investigation. Let the jurists, the moralists, and in general all who cultivate the speculative sciences, come and be initiated into countless data which for them will be so many mysteries: let them come and learn not only things, but method for examining and discovering other things: the method of observation, the rigorously analytic method, the only one that deserves the name of scientific, a spirit that is acquired only in the cultivation of the natural sciences and of their inseparable fellow workers, mathematics. There they will see the best application ever made of statistical, or rigorously numerical, procedures: this is the logic that the century in which we live demands, this is the fare that must be supplied to those who meditate on the lot of humanity, and on the most efficacious means of curing the moral ailments that afflict it. For the book of Mr. Parent is not merely an eminently moral book; from the first page to the last it vouches for its author as the most zealous advocate of good morals, as a most pure and undefiled soul, in spite of the infected breaths that the conscientious discharge of his most grave mission forced him to inhale from time to time over the long period of eight years. Well might this profound philosopher, this preacher of physical and

[p. 223]

> moral por texto á su precioso doctrinal aquel famoso " et nunc reges intelligite ; .. erudímini qui judicatis terram ! .. " Obras de esta especie son las que realizan la duda cartesia-na en la investigación , pues llamando á examen cuantas especies corren validas en la ciencia , antes de adoptar conclusión   alguna , se comienza á pensar de nuevo , proce-diendo cual si nada se supiera ; así es como quedan estirpa-dos infinitos errores que habían ya recibido la sanción del tiempo y de las más respetables autoridades . No por me-dios diversos de estos pudo otro profundo pensador , el no ménos que Parent malogrado Niebuhr , conmover hasta en sus cimientos el venerado monumento de la Historia Roma-na . Valiéndose de cuantos recursos puede suministrar la observación , llamando en su auxilio las ciencias , las artes , las lenguas , situándose en los mismos lugares en que pasa-ron los sucesos admirables de ese pueblo extraordinario , midiendo , contando y pesando ; así fué como se aparejó el profundo Niebuhr para acometer la ardua empresa : hasta no estar así surtido de datos , no intentó graduar y confron-tar entre sí los testimonios de los historiadores , escapando apenas uno de su severo espíritu analista , destructor á un tiempo de lo deleznable del edificio , y reconstructor de la obra con aquellos mismos fragmentos que pudieron quedar á toda prueba . Pero muy léjos me llevaría el querer citar las obras que en la época presente ofrecen el verdadero dechado del espíritu de investigación . Yo pondría de muy buena voluntad al lado de los que llevo citados los nombres no ménos dignos de un Juan Federico Herschell , de un Raspail , de un Tocqueville y de otros eminentes varones en gran número , aunque no tanto como vulgarmente se cree , que también en las ciencias hay vulgo y mucho vulgo , y no se cuentan á docenas las cabezas verdaderamente ori-ginales y escudriñadoras . De intento me he abstenido en lo que va dicho hasta ahora de incluir á la lógica entre las ciencias intelectuales que más deben á las naturales , por ser punto que reservo

moral health, have set as text to his precious doctrinal that famous “et nunc reges intelligite;.. erudímini qui judicatis terram!..” [and now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you that judge the earth!] It is works of this kind that put the Cartesian doubt into practice in investigation, for, calling to examination all the notions that pass current in science, before adopting any conclusion one begins to think anew, proceeding as if nothing were known; it is thus that countless errors are rooted out which had already received the sanction of time and of the most respectable authorities. Not by means other than these was another profound thinker, Niebuhr, cut off untimely no less than Parent, able to shake to its very foundations the venerated monument of Roman History.—Availing himself of every resource that observation can furnish, calling the sciences, the arts and the languages to his aid, placing himself in the very spots where the admirable events of that extraordinary people took place, measuring, counting and weighing: it was thus that the profound Niebuhr equipped himself to undertake the arduous enterprise: until he was thus supplied with data, he did not attempt to weigh and confront with one another the testimonies of the historians, scarcely one of them escaping his severe analytic spirit, at once the destroyer of what was crumbling in the edifice and the rebuilder of the work with those very fragments that proved able to stand every test. But it would carry me very far to try to cite the works that in the present age offer the true model of the spirit of investigation. I would very willingly place beside those I have cited the no less worthy names of a John Frederick Herschel, of a Raspail, of a Tocqueville and of other eminent men in great number, though not so great as is commonly believed, for in the sciences too there is a vulgar, and a large vulgar, and the truly original and searching heads are not counted by the dozen.

I have purposely abstained, in what has been said so far, from including logic among the intellectual sciences that owe most to the natural ones, because it is a point that I reserve

for a separate chapter in the refutation of one of the subsequent paragraphs of my esteemed correspondent; although further allegations on the matter might already be held superfluous, when one considers that psychology, the mother of true logic in the sense in which the Dómine and I understand the word, is also the mother of morality, legislation and the other speculative sciences to which our observations have been confined. But, having repeatedly promised to air the point separately, the Dómine may now count on another long entry in the record of services rendered by the experimental sciences to logic: rather, he will say, recalling my earlier expressions:—“that not even the science of Logic would exist, had it not been for the natural sciences themselves.” He will already be aware, from what has been said, of how well founded Bacon was when, in drawing up his table of the sciences, he set Logic in the penultimate place, ever consistent with the great principle that I stamped as an epigraph at the head of my Memoir, namely: “that even supposing its organon (that is, its method) to be absolute, it would avail nothing for the reform of the sciences without natural history (that is, without the physical, physiological and psychological facts, for a complete history must include them all); whereas that same history by itself, even without the organon, would contribute amply to the longed-for reform: for which reason it seemed more fitting and natural to occupy oneself wholly and before all else with so important a matter.”

Thus it will cause no little surprise to see how the intellectual sciences have been fertilized, or rather created, by the natural ones, practicing to the letter the profound maxims of Bacon, and all his prophecies being fulfilled, that there should still be in France, in enlightened France, not one but many men of letters who maintain that with the method of Verulam only the physical sciences have been created, but not the intellectual; as though there could be a good

[p. 225]
