Thus far, then, a debt of the moral science Psychology to the natural science Physiology; and I believe we shall be agreed; but if my adversary is not, he may let me know, so that I may proceed to a longer demonstration of that single particular, although many are the matters that call us. Logic. This, even taken in the strict sense of the formal laws of reasoning, has to be indebted to other branches; and if it is understood in the broad sense, which is how it is taught both in our courses and in those of Europe, and which for that very reason constitutes our principal question, there is scarcely an important chapter of it that does not derive light from, or is not wholly the offspring of, other sciences, and among them very directly of Psychology, Mathematics and Physics.—Both points have been demonstrated in my answer to the Dómine, although the second is still pending, because, not contenting myself with some examples (which is enough for my proof), I offered him a long list of debts, which I left interrupted. Now comes Metaphysics; and as regards it I have demonstrated, not only in my own opinion, but [p. 265] in that of the foremost experts, that it is today scarcely more than a desideratum: so many are the abstruse questions with which it has to occupy itself, many of which will probably remain forever insoluble, that some even deny it the name of science, though I am not of that number. Thus, as regards metaphysics properly so called, you will relieve me of further proof of its relatively backward state. We come now to Morality; and here is what has most dazzled you in the question, for you have said to yourself: How could Morality fail to be more advanced than the physical sciences, when without Morality societies cannot exist; when we find Morality even in the most barbarous hordes; when we find Morality cultivated with such brilliant success by the foremost minds of antiquity and from the remotest times; when without Morality responsibility cannot exist, and consequently it is eternal and invariable, deeply engraved in the heart of man, and independent of every system: see, in confirmation, to what high degree of science the Morality of the Crucified attained; whereas the conquests in the physical sciences have been the slow and protracted work of time, men having formed the most mistaken ideas of the causes of phenomena through a long course of centuries: witness, among innumerable others, the hypotheses on the system of the Universe until the coming of Copernicus into the world.—Nor will you throw it in my face that I weaken your reasons; for, without even finishing the dissection of the various members of your Achilles, I have strengthened him with the most powerful musculature that can be attached to him.—But in the first place it is necessary to distinguish between practical Morality and moral science, for plainly in some parts of the objection the word is taken in the first sense, and in others in the second. In this question, as in others of its kind, the unknown would always be much cleared up by fixing correctly the meaning in which the terms are taken: if the infant state of knowledge had been distinguished from its state of greater progress, and [p. 266] especially if due attention had been paid to the essential difference between communicating doctrines by mere authority (as happens in the cradle of society by means of religion) and investigating the principles, relations and causes of things by diligent study (which is what constitutes science), then the whole controversy would have come down to no more than a miserable play on words.— Indeed, no great progress in moral science is needed to know, for example, that death is an evil and life a good, illness an evil and health a good; for it is enough merely to have been born to feel it, and consequently nothing is more natural than that men, as a necessary consequence, should hold immoral whatever tends to destroy those goods or to foster those evils.—Here, then, we have Morality, which necessarily starts from our first impressions, without such a thing, nor even the code that might be founded on such bases, yet deserving the name of moral science. Unjust beyond measure would the Supreme Maker have been had he left the foundation of responsibility to the long lapse of time, or to the investigations of science, while making us responsible. Precisely the same, neither more nor less (though, strictly, rather more than less)—as we shall see presently—happens with the physical part. How much knowledge even the most savage man possesses of the nature that surrounds him, and how much and how many items of it he applies to his needs, getting the best out of them, without attaining to the true causes, without yet having the science, which consists in the doctrine, in the why of things and their relations— and here is how sometimes, not always, as I showed elsewhere, art naturally precedes science, the observation of facts always precedes reasoning. If we undertook even to make a brief survey of this physical knowledge of the savage, we should see how far it exceeds the intellectual and moral knowledge he possesses. He has a notion of foods and their action, he knows poisons and antidotes, he knows the seasons and their influence on his [p. 267] body and on vegetation, or on hunting and fishing; he builds himself a hut, although he is not yet an architect: he fills the need, but he has not yet arrived at art, nor at science. He knows the action of fire on bodies, he knows the qualities of certain animals, he measures time by means of the stars, and for that very reason studies their phases and respective positions, and yet he is still no astronomer: he knows a number of minerals, plants and animals, and yet he is no naturalist: he cures the ailments of his suffering brother by virtue of the secrets he possesses, and yet he is no physician; in short, if the most savage man were to set forth all he knows in regard to physical nature, and in great part even in regard to its causes and relations, it would be a matter for filling many volumes.—But why do I linger over this idle demonstration? Are the facts that serve as the basis of Morality, perchance, of an essentially different character? Is it not the impressions man receives that afford it its foundations? Is not reason the agent in both cases? We have, then, that it is very inexact to affirm that in the moral sciences we must know more because we carry within ourselves the instrument and the object of the science. It will be said that in respect of Morality and Legislation antiquity has left us monuments more finished, more scientific, than in the field of the natural sciences, as is proved by the political and religious systems of the Moseses, Lycurguses, Solons, Numas, the Roman legislation, and above all the very religion of the Crucified, without counting the respectable phalanx of celebrated and truly scientific works on Ethics, Politics and Legislation left us by the most eminent philosophers, Greek as well as Roman. Before answering this objection, allow me to recall that even if the case were such as it is represented, still all the monuments in moral and legislative science put together could not for an instant sustain the comparison, as regards scientific rigor, with Euclid’s elements of Geometry alone. And never forget, sir, this datum so precious for the [p. 268] question. Coming now to answer directly, I will say: that worthy to be set in comparison with those cited are the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus, of Epicurus, of Pythagoras, of Hippocrates and of Pliny on natural phenomena, and the discoveries made by the Egyptians and Greeks in Astronomy, in Geometry, in Music, and in general in the physico-mathematical sciences. Aristotle’s famous natural history alone is a treasure, inestimable not merely for its precious facts but for its admirable classification; a monument to which there is nothing to oppose, either ancient or modern, in the judgment of the first authority on the subject, Georges Cuvier: to Hippocrates, the first observer of antiquity, what do we oppose for his work de aëre, locis et aquis, considering the age of the world in the epoch he reached? And what shall we say of the immense knowledge in Mechanics, in Hydraulics and in all the auxiliary physico-mathematical sciences presupposed by those sumptuous monuments of Egyptian, Persian, Greek and Roman architecture? Let their temples and their palaces speak for me, their pyramids and sarcophagi, their roads and their canals, their aqueducts and their fountains, their ports and their ships. Only open the works of Vitruvius, and anyone will be astounded not only at the profound knowledge in the physical and mathematical sciences displayed by the eminent architect, but at the eminently scientific method with which they are set forth. Let their statues speak for me.... ah! their statues..... they speak well enough by themselves: has there ever been seen a delicacy, a finish greater than that offered by the sculpture of the Greeks? Who does not stand enraptured, pained, involuntarily mimicking the contortions of the priestly father, on contemplating the group of the Laocoön! Who had a more intimate feeling for nature, or how could it have been reached except by the most minute observation of external forms, of physical facts?— Canova, the first artist of the age, would fling away his chisel in despair each time he looked at one of those fragments [p. 269] rescued by England from the ruins of the Parthenon: and with reason, for I, merely from seeing those majestic figures from behind, would stand astounded at the expression of their air and attitudes, and absorbed in contemplating the superhuman power by which it had been possible to animate those colossal stones in that manner. “Potens est homo de lapidibus istis suscitare (non filios Abrahæ— apage!) sed filios animæ suæ.” [Man is able of these stones to raise up (not children unto Abraham—away with that!) but children of his own soul.]— Let even the relics unearthed from Pompeii and Herculaneum speak for me with regard to their artifacts, and there will be observed, in works of necessity as in those of mere ornament, for public and for domestic use, in metals as in stones, an exquisite taste and finish, which will always be the delight no less than the despair of modern craftsmen.—What physical knowledge of bodies and their laws do these arts not presuppose? The very arts of war, all founded on physical knowledge—to what state of advancement did they not attain among those notable peoples of antiquity? Gymnastics, to which the ancients gave so much importance, not only as a powerful weapon of war, but very especially on account of the influence of the physical on the moral, which they perceived from the remotest times (“mens sana in corpore sano” [a sound mind in a sound body]), offers another precious argument of the height their knowledge of nature had reached. But... nature.... who knew her better, or who was more worthy to be her interpreter, than the most sweet Virgil? The Georgics are the most precious treatise on agriculture that antiquity has transmitted to us, a treatise of which the whole work de Re rustica of the celebrated Columella is a no less important commentary. It would be difficult to present a book of any epoch more finished than the Georgics; and here we leave aside the poetic merit, on which head it has no rival, and consider it merely as a most vast treasury of observations as well gathered as they are arranged.—And since it is a matter of displaying works finished in their kind, and in the matter of sciences of observation [p. 270] (let me be allowed a certain disorder in my ideas, caused by the haste with which I write, since it in no way harms clarity, the only target that must not be lost sight of in writings of this kind), let the competent declare whether there are many to set beside the Geography of Strabo: full knowledge of the subject, wealth of observations, solid judgment, measure, discernment, are gifts that vie with one another throughout the work, and make us feel at every step, as happens to us with regard to so many other branches, the infinite important works of the ancients that we have lost forever; for it must not be forgotten that we still cannot but judge them in a very incomplete manner, very often almost groping, at other times entirely in the dark, and in no case with that full knowledge of the matter that right and just criticism demands. These considerations lead me as if by the hand to touch briefly on the physical knowledge presupposed in the ancients by the practice of the conjuring arts—of magic, I mean—which the priests employed to support their oracles, and to maintain and give credit to their empire over souls in order to govern bodies. There will scarcely be anyone who has not glanced at something about the miracles of Apollonius of Tyana and other impostors, miracles very particularly spread abroad by Philostratus, and of which much of the same style may be seen in Lucian, Flavius Josephus and other writers of antiquity. These soothsayers or priests had of necessity to appeal to astronomy and to knowledge of the atmosphere in order to foretell celestial and meteorological phenomena with such exactness as might give them a divine investiture. “The power of bringing down fire from the heavens, even in circumstances in which the electrical influence was at rest,” says Sir David Brewster, “could not but be regarded solely as a heavenly gift. Another irresistible instrument of imposture must have been offered them by the power of rendering the human body insensible to fire; and in the combinations of chemistry and the influence of soporific drugs and embrocations the [p. 271] ancient magicians no doubt found their most profitable means of deluding.”

The secret use they made of scientific discoveries has in great part prevented their procedures from coming down to us; but although we are very ill informed regarding the progress of the ancients in the various departments of the physical sciences, we nevertheless have sufficient proofs to affirm “that almost all the branches of knowledge contribute their marvels to make up the stock of the magician, so that some idea may even be obtained of the scientific acquisitions of primitive times by means of a diligent study of their fables and miracles.” There is not a single branch that did not pay them its tribute; acoustics, hydrostatics, mechanics, and especially optics were in their hands an inexhaustible mine of the deceptions they sought.—Were I not afraid of extending myself too far, I would gladly extract a thousand passages, from Pliny especially, in confirmation of all that has been said.

II. (1)

I will say more: until the moderns themselves had advanced considerably in the study of the phenomena of nature, they went on denying various facts related in the most authentic manner by the ancient historians, among others the existence of aerolites, or stones fallen from the atmosphere, to which the aforesaid Pliny alludes, and which no one doubts nowadays, any more than the famous burning mirrors with which Archimedes set fire to the fleet of the enemies of his country, stationed at a great distance from the shore. The same has happened with countless passages of Herodotus, whose history may be considered in great part as a precious narrative of his own travels rather than as an account of things past, and is for that very reason extremely

(1) Diario de la Habana of February 23, 1839.—(A. Z.)

[p. 272]

> importante como colección de observaciones                sobre todas materias . El modo de instruirse de los filósofos antiguos , era el medio más seguro de que se ocupasen tanto en cuestio-nes puramente físicas como morales , pues ninguno de ellos consideraba su educación terminada , si no llevaba el com-plemento ó última mano de los viajes ; no contentándose los más con una simple recorrida de los paises que visitaban , trasladábanse á ellos con ánimo de estudiar á fondo su na-turaleza física y moral , fijándose con preferencia en aque-llos más célebres por sus adelantos en las ciencias , como lo hicieron los griegos respecto del Egipto , de donde saca-ron rica mies para las naturales Thales Milesio , Pitágo-ras y otros de menos nombradía . De este último        es bien sabido que hasta columbró el verdadero sistema del mun-do , después revivido por Copérnico ; ( 1) y de Epicuro puede decirse que ofrece los lineamentos de la teoría Newtoniana en cuanto al sistema de atracción universal , y de la química moderna en cuanto á la teoría atomística , á no juzgar más que por la exposición que hace de sus doctrinas su discípu-lo Lucrecio en el poema " De rerum natura " . Admiran ver-daderamente los pasajes en que se notan estas coinciden-cias , sin que por eso pretendamos que Newton y los quími-cos modernos fuesen á aprender química en Epicuro ni en Lucrecio : se trata tan solo de mostrar la altura á que en ciencias físicas se elevaron los filósofos antiguos . Pero ¿qué más ni mejor prueba de que todos los pueblos principiaron por las ciencias físicas que sus mismos siste-mas religiosos primitivos , fundados todos en los sistemas cosmogónicos , que en sus vedas y mithas , ó misterios y ale- (1) A este propósito podría también citar el tan famoso como di-vulgado pasaje de Séneca el trágico , que comienza “ venient annis sé-cula seris , " en el cual se vaticina la existencia del nuevo mundo del modo más terminante y circunstanciado . Si yo quisiera valerme de los recursos con que brinda la erudición moderna, ahí está el alemán Hee-ren , que me suministraría datos estupendos sobre las navegaciones de los Fenicios , y en general sobre las relaciones mercantiles de los pue-blos de la antigüedad , y los progresos consiguientes  en las artes y ra-mos que ellas presuponían   .

important as a collection of observations on all matters. The ancient philosophers’ manner of instructing themselves was the surest means of their occupying themselves with purely physical questions as much as with moral ones; for none of them considered his education finished if it had not received the complement or finishing touch of travel; most of them, not content with a simple tour of the countries they visited, removed to them with the intention of studying thoroughly their physical and moral nature, fixing by preference on those most celebrated for their advances in the sciences, as the Greeks did with respect to Egypt, whence Thales of Miletus, Pythagoras and others of less renown drew a rich harvest for the natural sciences. Of this last it is well known that he even glimpsed the true system of the world, afterwards revived by Copernicus; (1) and of Epicurus it may be said that he offers the outlines of the Newtonian theory as regards the system of universal attraction, and of modern chemistry as regards the atomic theory, to judge only by the exposition of his doctrines given by his disciple Lucretius in the poem “De rerum natura.” The passages in which these coincidences are noticed are truly admirable, without our claiming on that account that Newton and the modern chemists went to learn chemistry from Epicurus or from Lucretius: it is only a question of showing the height to which the ancient philosophers rose in the physical sciences.

But what more or better proof that all peoples began with the physical sciences than their very primitive religious systems, all founded on the cosmogonic systems which, in their Vedas and myths, or mysteries and alle-

(1) On this subject I might also cite the passage of Seneca the tragedian, as famous as it is widely known, which begins “venient annis sæcula seris,” [there will come, in late years, an age] in which the existence of the new world is foretold in the most decisive and circumstantial manner. If I wished to avail myself of the resources that modern erudition offers, there is the German Heeren, who would furnish me astonishing data on the navigations of the Phoenicians, and in general on the commercial relations of the peoples of antiquity, and the consequent progress in the arts and branches which those relations presupposed.

[p. 273]

> gorías , nos ofrecen los más antiguos ? Ahí están el Egipto y la India señaladamente para convencernos de que desde la cuna de la sociedad , desde los tiempos fabulosos , apare-cen mezcladas las cuestiones metafisicas y religiosas con la exposición de los fenómenos del mundo físico , ó por mejor decir , como una consecuencia inmediata la parte metafísica y moral del conocimiento del universo material ; advirtién-donos así naturaleza , en todo y por todo , que no podemos elevarnos á lo espiritual sino por la escala de lo corpóreo . ¡Qué fácil me sería dejarme correr disertando por este cam-po riquísimo , y aprovechándome de las luces que sobre él han derramado así los más hábiles orientalistas como los primeros filósofos de la culta Europa ! Sólo la historia de la Astronomía bastaría para convencer hasta qué punto asombroso de adelanto arribaron los antiguos en las cien-cias físico - matemáticas . Pero son suficientes estas indica-ciones para mi propósito ; que no ha sido por cierto ventilar la cuestión de superioridad entre antiguos y modernos , sino únicamente demostrar que estabar aquellos más adelanta-dos en las ciencias físicas de lo que cree el erudito articu-lista , y al mismo tiempo que todos los pueblos siguen for-zosamente la ley de la naturaleza de comenzar por el prin-cipio , ó sea , recibir impresiones antes de reflejarlas , observar y conocer la naturaleza exterior antes de conocerse á sí mis-mos . Si tal no fuera , ni sentido tendría el famoso nosce te ipsum de los griegos , pues el predicárseles que se estudia-sen á si mismos , prueba que engolfados en la investigación del mundo exterior se habían olvidado de la importantísima de su interior .  Tampoco se esplicaría mejor la memorable revolución causada por Sócrates , la que sería en ese caso un efecto sin causa , toda vez que él no hizo más que atraer los ánimos , enfrascados en la indagación de la naturaleza externa , al estudio de la moral , con el consejo y el ejemplo . Pero ¿ puede la moral aislarse de lo fisico , y aislarse con ventaja para su estudio ? De ninguna manera : pues así co-mo en el estudio de nuestras facultades mentales hemos 18

gories, the most ancient of them offer us? There are Egypt and India, notably, to convince us that from the cradle of society, from fabulous times, metaphysical and religious questions appear mingled with the exposition of the phenomena of the physical world, or, better said, the metaphysical and moral part appears as an immediate consequence of the knowledge of the material universe; nature thus warning us, in each and every thing, that we cannot rise to the spiritual except by the ladder of the corporeal. How easy it would be for me to let myself run on, discoursing over this most rich field, and availing myself of the lights shed upon it by the ablest Orientalists as well as by the foremost philosophers of cultivated Europe! The history of Astronomy alone would suffice to convince anyone to what astonishing point of advancement the ancients attained in the physico-mathematical sciences. But these indications are sufficient for my purpose; which has certainly not been to air the question of superiority between ancients and moderns, but only to demonstrate that the former were more advanced in the physical sciences than the learned writer of the article believes, and at the same time that all peoples necessarily follow the law of nature, of beginning at the beginning, that is, of receiving impressions before reflecting upon them, of observing and knowing external nature before knowing themselves. Were it not so, the famous nosce te ipsum [know thyself] of the Greeks would have no meaning, for the preaching to them that they should study themselves proves that, engulfed in the investigation of the external world, they had forgotten the most important investigation of their inner one. Nor would the memorable revolution caused by Socrates be any better explained, for it would in that case be an effect without a cause, since all he did was to draw minds, absorbed in the inquiry into external nature, to the study of morals, by counsel and example.

But can morality be isolated from the physical, and isolated with advantage for its study? By no means: for just as in the study of our mental faculties we have

[p. 274]

> tenido que invocar las luces de la Fisiología , aunque no sea más que para deslindar los efectos que pertenecen al ins-tinto de los que corresponden á la conciencia ; de la misma suerte , en la moral , donde se deben primeramente describir nuestras pasiones y las causas que las apagan y fomentar , es de necesidad apelar á aquella misma ciencia preciosa para determinar el influjo de los órganos y funciones cor-porales sobre nuestros afectos morales , cuyo estudio presu-pone el de la Física propiamente tal , no menos que el de la Patología , ó conocimiento de los desórdenes de las funcio-nes , toda vez que no es dable conocer bien al hombre sano sin conocer bien al enfermo , y vice - versa ; tocándose aquí , como sucede á cada paso , apenas se profundiza cualquier ramo del saber humano , el estrecho enlace que existe entre ellos , no habiendo en rigor más que una ciencia , dividida y diversificada á causa de la limitación de nuestras faculta-des , tan fuera de proporción con la inmensidad de la natu-raleza . Dije y probé , que solo el capítulo de la enagenación mental daría importantes lecciones así al psicólogo como al moralista y al jurisconsulto , sobre los puntos más delica-dos de sus respectivas especialidades . Todo lo cual prueba que la perfección de la Moral en gran parte correrá parejas con los progresos en este ramo de las ciencias naturales . ¿De dónde , sino de la falta de Fisiología , así en la Psicología como en la Ética , pende que se hayan trasmitido grandes problemas de estas dos ciencias , de generación á generación , dándoseles diversa solución , según lo indican los varios sis-temas que en ellas han reinado , sin atinar con la verdadera ? Por otra parte , nadie que reflexione sobre la historia de las revoluciones humanas podrá desconocer que la Moral , como ciencia , se perfecciona de la propia manera que las otras , siendo tan hija de la observacion y la experiencia como cualquiera de las más esperimentales ; con sólo la par-ticularidad de que amenudo , amen de los siglos que suele aguardar por sus descubrimientos , ( en lo que también se parece bastante á las físicas ) todavía cuesta torrentes de

had to invoke the light of Physiology, if only to mark off the effects that belong to instinct from those that pertain to consciousness; in the same way, in Ethics, where our passions must first be described, together with the causes that extinguish and foster them, it is necessary to appeal to that same precious science to determine the influence of the bodily organs and functions upon our moral affections, the study of which presupposes that of Physics properly so called, no less than that of Pathology, or the knowledge of the disorders of the functions, since it is not possible to know the healthy man well without knowing the sick man well, and vice versa; here we touch, as happens at every step the moment one goes deep into any branch of human knowledge, upon the close connection that exists among them all, there being, strictly speaking, but one science, divided and diversified by reason of the limitation of our faculties, so out of proportion with the immensity of nature. I said and proved that the chapter on mental alienation alone would give important lessons to the psychologist as well as to the moralist and the jurist, upon the most delicate points of their respective specialties. All of which proves that the perfection of Ethics will in great part keep pace with the progress made in this branch of the natural sciences. From what, if not from the want of Physiology, in Psychology as well as in Ethics, does it come that great problems of these two sciences have been handed down from generation to generation, receiving diverse solutions, as the various systems that have reigned in them show, without hitting upon the true one?

On the other hand, no one who reflects upon the history of human revolutions can fail to recognize that Ethics, as a science, is perfected in the same manner as the others, being as much the daughter of observation and experience as any of the most experimental; with only this peculiarity, that often, besides the centuries it is wont to wait for its discoveries (in which it also bears a good resemblance to the physical sciences), the establishment of any new principle, however profitable it may be to humanity, still costs torrents of

[p. 275]

> sangre el establecimiento de cualquier nuevo principio por provechoso que sea á la humanidad . Y después de esta-blecido nada parece más natural ni más conforme á la ra-zón , asombrándose muy amenudo la generación subsecuen-te de que costase tan caro la adopción de una gran verdad en el orden moral . Yo no alcanzo como , concediéndose que la Ética es una ciencia de observación , y por lo mismo su-ceptible de progreso , que está enlazada con otras y máxime dependiente de la Ideología , no alcanzo , digo , como pueda negarse que la moral se variará ó corregirá , según los pro-gresos de las ciencias físicas , tanto más cuanto que para graduar ciertas acciones es forzoso conocer sus causas . No se crea , ni por un instante , que tratemos nosotros de incul-car que sean variables los eternos é inalterables principios de la ley moral , grabada en el corazón del hombre . Un ejemplo hará comprender nuestra idea : por la que se ha-bían formado los pueblos de la agorería , v . g . , se condenaba á muerte , aún entre las naciones cristianas ( 1) á los reos de este deiito enorme , según su legislación , que es siempre la expresión de las opiniones dominantes , base indispensa-ble de su moral ; siendo en esto muy consecuentes los hom-bres de entonces , pues partiendo del principio de ser la ayorería un pacto con el demonio , y por ende la más grave ofensa á la Divinidad , no le hallaban pena proporcionada y todo les parecía poco para el tamaño del delito . Viene la antorcha de las ciencias físicas á ilustrar los entendimientos sobre sus verdaderas causas humanas y muy humanas , nada de divinas ni diabólicas , y el pretendido crímen queda redu-cido á un pecadillo de charlatanismo . ¿Hay más que ten-der la vista sobre la larga historia de las humanas supersti-ciones , para multiplicar los ejemplos de este género ? Así , lejos de ser estraño , está en la naturaleza de las co-sas , no ya que varíe la moral , ó sean los principios de ac-ción de pueblos diversos , constituidos bajo distintas cir- (1) Apenas hace un siglo que se condenó el último , y no en España sino en Escocia .

blood. And once it is established nothing seems more natural or more in keeping with reason, the following generation very often marveling that the adoption of a great truth in the moral order should have cost so dear. I do not see how, granting that Ethics is a science of observation, and for that very reason susceptible of progress, that it is linked with others and above all dependent on Ideology, I do not see, I say, how it can be denied that morality will vary or be corrected according to the progress of the physical sciences, all the more since, in order to grade certain actions, it is necessary to know their causes. Let no one believe, not for an instant, that we are trying to inculcate that the eternal and unalterable principles of the moral law, engraved upon the heart of man, are variable. An example will make our idea understood: by reason of the idea that peoples had formed of sorcery, for instance, those guilty of this enormous crime were condemned to death, even among Christian nations, (1) according to their legislation, which is always the expression of the dominant opinions, the indispensable basis of their morality; the men of that time being in this very consistent, for, starting from the principle that sorcery was a pact with the devil, and hence the gravest offense against the Divinity, they found no proportionate penalty for it, and everything seemed to them too little for the magnitude of the crime. Then comes the torch of the physical sciences to enlighten minds as to its true causes, human and very human, nothing divine or diabolical about them, and the pretended crime is reduced to a little sin of charlatanism. Need one do more than cast one’s eye over the long history of human superstitions to multiply examples of this kind?

Thus, far from being strange, it is in the nature of things, not merely that morality, or rather the principles of action of diverse peoples, constituted under different cir-

(1) Barely a century ago the last was condemned, and not in Spain but in Scotland.

[p. 276]

> cunstancias , pero hasta las de un mismo pueblo en los varios siglos de su existencia , no ofreciendo la Historia fe-nómeno mas constante que ese contínuo cambiar de los . resortes que mueven á la humanidad ----Compárese la Edad Media con el siglo XVIII , y este con el presente , en las na-ciones cristianas , y si se quiere en una sola de dichas na-ciones . Todas ellas , y señaladamente la Francia , se desvi-vian en el siglo XII por pasar á Tierra Santa á la conquista del sepulcro de Cristo , y esa misma nación en el XVIII ya no siente el sacro fuego de la religión que le hizo obrar pro-digios en los campos de Palestina , pero en su lugar arras-trada por otro estímulo ejecuta hazañas no ménos porten-tosas , presentando un muro de pechos á toda la Europa armada contra ella . ¿Y moverían esos mismos resortes , y caso de mover moverian del propio modo que antes , á -la Francia del siglo decimo nono ? Nadie discrepa en la res-puesta negativa : permitiéndoseme , sin embargo , observar que en medio de tanta variación é instabilidad es uno mismo-inalterable el corazón del hombre ; cambian en él las ideas pero permanecen las facultades , que le son congénitas , in-herentes á su naturaleza ; en el fondo así de las cruzadas como de las campañas de la revolución , vemos el mismo entusiasmo , la misma suceptibilidad  aplicada á diversos objetos , y fomentada con diverso pávulo . Si nada sucede en vano en la naturaleza de las cosas , y si la historia es el teatro donde figura la humanidad , nada más conforme que esas variaciones , que en último análisis son otro nombre para decir progreso , puesto que la misma naturaleza pa-rece marcarnos con el dedo que cada idea ó resorte , una vez lleno su destino , no tiene para que reaparecer en la es--cena , ó por lo ménos , haciéndo el papel principal que antes desempeñara . Solo de esta manera es como puede esplicarse la historia , pues de otra suerte los hechos serían efectos sin causa : en pos de la licencia del siglo XVIII vino forzosa-mente la moderación del XIX . ( 1 ) ( 1) Cosa singular .   Cousin que esplica del mismo modo la historia , [p. 277] Pero ¿que necesidad habia de acudir á la historia en la cuestión presente , cuando el más sencillo razonamiento por sí solo basta á dejarla para siempre dirimida ?   Las ideas influyen eficazmente en las acciones , pues que el hombre opera según crée ; es así que las ideas cambian al infinito , luego las acciones han de seguir la propia suerte . Variará la ciencia moral precisamente en virtud de haber adelan-tado los conocimientos físicos , y por fuerza variará la prác-tica , esto es las costumbres . Quiero poner otro ejemplo luminoso antes de pasar á desenvolver nuevas ideas . Ya se habrá notado que los escojo de aquellos que demuestran no solo cambio en la legislación sino tambien en la moral como consecuencia fatal de haber variado la opinión , así para no dar entrada á nuevas dudas , como por la inapreciable ventaja de patenti-zar las estrechas relaciones entre una y otra ciencia , vinien-donos á convencer al cabo de que el código civil de un pueblo es igualmente su código moral , lo cual solo sucede por copiarse en él exacta y fielmente el estado de la opi-nión . Desde la hora y punto que esta varía , ya es muerta la letra de la ley, existe escrita todavía pero con el mismo género de existencia para el pueblo de que se trate que otra cualquiera ley de Licurgo ó de Solón ; permanece en el papel pero no gobierna , no se toma por tipo de las acciones -de los individuos , ni por regla para las determinaciones de la autoridad . Pero vamos al ejemplo ofrecido , y que nos lo proporciona la usura . No solo por ilegal , sino por pe-caminoso se tenía en todas las naciones cristianas el más ligero aumento á lo fijado por la ley en el interés del dine-ro , á pesar de las vicisitudes que naturalmente ofrece el co-mercio , verdadero océano que tan pronto retira sus olas de la ribera dejándola enjuta como las hace retroceder para no admite el sensualismo : los fenómenos   en todos los ramos son causa y ocasión de las nociones .   No quiero disertar ahora , sino marcar una contradicción , no se creyera que estaba en mí , que he combatido otras doctrinas del mismo autor .

cumstances, should vary, but even those of one and the same people in the various centuries of its existence, History offering no phenomenon more constant than that continual changing of the springs that move humanity.—Compare the Middle Ages with the eighteenth century, and this with the present one, among the Christian nations, and, if you will, in a single one of those nations. All of them, and France most notably, were wild in the twelfth century to cross to the Holy Land for the conquest of the sepulcher of Christ; and that same nation in the eighteenth no longer feels the sacred fire of the religion that made it work prodigies on the fields of Palestine, but in its stead, carried along by another stimulus, performs deeds no less portentous, presenting a wall of breasts to all Europe in arms against it. And would those same springs move, and in case they moved, would they move in the same way as before, the France of the nineteenth century? No one dissents from the negative answer: allowing me, however, to observe that in the midst of so much variation and instability the heart of man is one and the same, unalterable; ideas change in it, but the faculties remain, which are congenital to it, inherent in its nature; at the bottom of the crusades as well as of the campaigns of the revolution we see the same enthusiasm, the same susceptibility applied to diverse objects and fed with diverse fuel. If nothing happens in vain in the nature of things, and if history is the theater where humanity plays its part, nothing could be more fitting than those variations, which in the last analysis are another name for progress, since nature herself seems to point out to us with her finger that each idea or spring, once its destiny is fulfilled, has no reason to reappear upon the scene, or at least not playing the principal part it played before. Only in this manner can history be explained, for otherwise the facts would be effects without a cause: after the license of the eighteenth century there necessarily came the moderation of the nineteenth. (1) [p. 277] But what need was there to resort to history in the present question, when the simplest reasoning by itself suffices to leave it settled forever? Ideas influence actions effectively, since man acts according as he believes; but ideas change infinitely; therefore actions must follow the same fate. The science of morals will vary precisely by virtue of the advance of physical knowledge, and of necessity the practice, that is, manners and customs, will vary.

(1) A singular thing. Cousin, who explains history in the same way,

I wish to give another luminous example before passing on to develop new ideas. It will already have been noticed that I choose them from among those that show a change not only in legislation but also in morality, as the inevitable consequence of a change of opinion, both so as to give no entrance to new doubts and for the inestimable advantage of making plain the close relations between the one science and the other, bringing us in the end to be convinced that the civil code of a people is likewise its moral code, which happens only because the state of opinion is copied in it exactly and faithfully. From the very hour and moment that opinion varies, the letter of the law is dead; it still exists in writing, but with the same kind of existence, for the people in question, as any law whatever of Lycurgus or of Solon; it remains on paper but does not govern, it is not taken as the pattern for the actions of individuals, nor as the rule for the determinations of authority.—But let us come to the example promised, which is furnished us by usury. Not only as illegal, but as sinful, was the slightest increase in the interest of money above what the law had fixed held in all Christian nations, in spite of the vicissitudes that commerce naturally presents, a veritable ocean that now withdraws its waves from the shore, leaving it dry, now drives them back to does not admit sensationalism: the phenomena in every branch are the cause and occasion of the notions.—I do not wish to hold forth now, but only to point out a contradiction, lest it be thought that it lay in me, who have combated other doctrines of the same author.

[p. 278]

> inundarla . Como este principio cívico - moral dependía del concepto en que estaban los pueblos cristianos , fué menes-ter que variase este concepto para que dejase de gobernar aquel tipo ; presentando el mismo aumento del comercio en-tre los hombres nuevas combinaciones , nuevos fenómenos mercantiles , fué puesto en evidencia el hecho general de que al dinero le sucedía lo que á cualquier otro género en el mercado , " que vale mucho si anda escaso , y vale poco si corre abundante " , y desde ese momento quedó derogada la ley moral , y barrenada la ley civil . ¿ Con qué derecho , con qué justicia se pudo exigir á un prestamista que diera ba-rato su metálico , al paso que se le pedía más caro por otro artículo ? Esta sencilla reflexión basta para patentizar la fuerza de la injusticia que le infiriera semejante legislación . Y tal es el imperio de la demostración , que los tribunales más respetables del mundo civilizado , tiempo há que en punto á usuras , sin estar derogadas aquellas leyes , declaran muy lícito un interés mayor que el legal , según las circuns--tancias del mercado en la época del contrato . ¿ Son és--tas ó no , conquistas , y grandes conquistas , de la cien-cia ?     Pero ¡ qué triunfos tan bien y tan trabajosamente al-canzados ! ¿ Por ventura se han obtenido así sencillamente con solo asomar la idea madre de todos ellos , ó han sido el resultado de largas discusiones , prolongadas hasta por si-glos y manejadas por las plumas más elocuentes , por las plumas de los bienhechores , de los moralizadores del linaje humano ? Y ved aquí lo que distingue á los progresos de las ciencias morales , como ya indiqué , que por fuerza han de ser más lentos , dado que sus experiencias no pueden ser tan perceptibles ni tan prontas como las que efectuamos en los laboratorios . Aun en las ciencias físico - matemáticas se nota que aquellos puntos que no pueden someterse tan. pronto ni tan fácilmente á la experiencia , por contrariar al primitivo   ó más grosero testimonio de los sentidos , son más difíciles de establecer fuera de duda , como aconteció con el sistema Copernicano . Aquí mismo se advierte la [p. 279] mayor facilidad con que se adapta el precioso instrumento de las matemáticas    á las ciencias naturales que no á las morales , sin dar á entender por esto que no sea aplicable también á las últimas , pues lo es en bastante grado , y aun ese será uno de los medios más eficaces para su progreso . (1 ) Reflexionemos todavía acerca del ejemplo presentado , y veremos si es fecundo en consecuencias aplicables al asun-to principal . El prueba que no basta toda la fuerza del in-genio humano para descubrir ciertas verdades , por obvias que después de encontradas parezcan á los que , aprovechan-dose de ellas , no tuvieron el trabajo de buscarlas , sino que es necesario que las circunstancias hayan desenvuelto los hechos á tin de que haciéndose estos más perceptibles , re-caigan sobre ellos las observaciones , para después formar la ciencia . Recordará el lector , como dije al Dómine , que ni aún podía concebirse la existencia de las ciencias especula-tivas , ó que era forzoso considerarlas como efecto sin cau-sa , sinó eran producidas con ocasión de las mismas necesi-dades del hombre , y así esplicaba el nacimiento de la Geo-metría . flood it. As this civic-moral principle depended on the conception the Christian peoples held, it was necessary that this conception should vary in order for that standard to cease to govern; the very increase of commerce among men presenting new combinations, new mercantile phenomena, the general fact was made evident that the same thing happened to money as to any other commodity in the market, “that it is worth much if it is scarce, and worth little if it runs abundant,” and from that moment the moral law was abrogated and the civil law undermined. With what right, with what justice could a lender be required to give his coin cheap, while he was asked a higher price for any other article? This simple reflection is enough to make plain the force of the injustice that such legislation inflicted upon him. And such is the empire of demonstration that the most respected tribunals of the civilized world have long since, in the matter of usury, without those laws being repealed, declared a higher interest than the legal one quite lawful, according to the circumstances of the market at the time of the contract. Are these, or are they not, conquests, and great conquests, of science? But what triumphs, so well and so laboriously won! Were they perchance obtained thus simply, merely by the appearance of the idea that is mother of them all, or have they been the result of long discussions, prolonged even for centuries and handled by the most eloquent pens, by the pens of the benefactors, of the moralizers of the human race? And see here what distinguishes the progress of the moral sciences, as I have already indicated: it must of necessity be slower, given that their experiments cannot be so perceptible nor so prompt as those we perform in the laboratories. Even in the physico-mathematical sciences it is noticeable that those points which cannot be submitted so soon or so easily to experiment, because they run counter to the primitive or grosser testimony of the senses, are more difficult to establish beyond doubt, as happened with the Copernican system. Here too one observes the [p. 279] greater ease with which the precious instrument of mathematics adapts itself to the natural sciences than to the moral ones, without meaning by this that it is not applicable to the latter also, for it is so in a considerable degree, and that will even be one of the most effective means for their progress. (1)

Let us reflect further upon the example presented, and we shall see whether it is fertile in consequences applicable to the main subject. It proves that the whole force of human genius is not enough to discover certain truths, however obvious they may seem, once found, to those who, profiting by them, had not the labor of seeking them; but that it is necessary for circumstances to have unfolded the facts, so that, these becoming more perceptible, observations may bear upon them, and the science may afterwards be formed. The reader will remember how I told the Dómine that the existence of the speculative sciences could not even be conceived, or that they would have to be considered as an effect without a cause, unless they were produced on occasion of man’s own needs; and thus I explained the birth of Geometry.

In the same way, Political Economy was born precisely in Great Britain, where there was bound to be more occasion for speculating on these matters, by virtue of the greater expansion and development that the industrial arts and mercantile dealings had in that field. In no other way has the Jurisprudence of modern nations been formed in great part. The same happens in Politics; if revolutions do not unfold certain facts, in vain would human reason strive to foresee them and prevent them.

(1) The experience I have in polemics of this kind obliges me at times to enter into explanations so obvious that to many they will seem needless, and that to me, besides being needless, seem tiresome: for in truth it would be delightful to speak not merely as little as possible, but even by formulas, if it can be done, in scientific matters; but however precious such a method of exposition may be, everything is relative in this world, and everything must be subordinated to the indispensable law of saying as much as is necessary, above all when unfortunately it is still necessary after more than the usual has been said.

[p. 280]

> barlos . Las mismas instituciones civiles y políticas pue-den y deben considerarse como verdaderos ensayos ó ex-perimentos , que andando el tiempo nos revelan los resulta-dos que no podríamos esperar , y que á veces ni pudimos pronosticar . Bien sentían la fuerza de estas verdades los formadores de la constitución anglo - americana , pues siem-pre la han caracterizado con el expresivo epíteto de nues-tro gran experimento . Con efecto , aun siendo una repúbli-ca el gobierno político de los Estados  Unidos , ¿ qué puntos de  semejenza  median entre ella y las repúblicas   de la anti-güedad ? ¡ Qué diversidad de elementos físicos , morales y políticos no juegan en uno y otro caso ! No es necesario más qué apuntar el paralelo para sacar las consecuencias . ¿No quedaron en este solo ejemplo desconcertadas todas las teorías de la antiguedad en materias gubernativas ? No porque ellas sean acreedoras á nuestro menosprecio , sino porque no habiendo tenido sus autores á la vista estos nue-vos hechos no pudieron despertárseles las ideas consiguien-tes . Si tal no fuera , ¿qué negocio más sencillo habría que el de gobernar á los pueblos ? Pero desgraciadamente es el más difícil de todos , como que más que ninguno reclama los costosos y largos frutos de la experiencia en el orden mo-ral . ¿Por qué oimos repetirá cada paso que la revolución fran-cesa es el libro más instructivo para los que dirigen las nacio-nes ? Porque ella desconcertó innumerables doctrinas recibi-das , y fué madre fecunda de otras infinitas á que no hubiera podido llegar toda la perspicacia del ingenio humano , dedica-do exclusivamente por siglos á especular sobre estas mate-rias . Tenemos pues , que en Moral , en Jurisprudencia , en Economía pública , en Política, lo mismo que en cualquier otro ramo experimental preceden los hechos á las disposi-ciones , las experiencias á las doctrinas , las causas á los efectos : siendo de notar precisamente que cuando se pres-cinde de este método natural , y se trata de adivinar en vez de acertar ó deducir , lo que se logra es que las ciencias es-peculativas se estacionen y aun retrograden en vez de ade [p. 281] lantar .   Y ved aquí cabalmente la tacha que ponerse suele á los filósofos antiguos , que en sus síntesis atrevidas se en-cumbraban por los campos imaginarios , olvidándose del te-rreno firme de los hechos . ¡Cuanto más no hubieran pro-gresado los griegos con sus brillantes disposiciones hasta en las ciencias experimentales , si hubiesen siempre seguido esta senda ! Pero una vez vista por los modernos la efica . cia de semejante método en dichas ciencias , no han podido menos , máxime tocando la identidad de orígen en todas ellas , de suspirar por su aplicación á las llamadas impro-piamente morales ó especulativas , para imprimirles una marcha más firme y rigurosa , prenda segura de sus ulterio-res adelantamientos . Y heme aquí naturalmente conducido á resolver otra de las dudas del Sr. Adicto , sobre el atraso en que afirmé se hallaban comparativamente las ciencias morales respecto de las físicas y matemáticas ; pues en cuanto a ser ciencias de observación y susceptibles de progreso , no obstante des-cansar en algunos principios tan inalterables como univer-sales , no puede quedar ya ni sombra de duda aun al enten-dimiento más prevenido . Antes de ventilar este punto permitame el Señor Contrin-cante le recuerde que bajo el nombre de ciencias mora-les se comprenden en general todos aquellos ramos de los conocimientos humanos en que no se hacen materialmente experimentos y observaciones con los instrumentos y reacti-vos , como se practican en las llamadas naturales . Es tan-to más necesario este recuerdo cuanto que Adicto casi ha contraido su argumentación , para demostrar la perfección á que en su concepto han llegado las ciencias morales , á la Moral misma y á la Jurisprudencia ; debiendo tener presen-te que aún cuando dichas dos ciencias se hallasen realmente en el estado de adelanto que pretende , todavía esta demos-tración no infirmaría en lo más leve el aserto general de que las ciencias llamadas morales se hallan en atraso res-pecto de las naturales , pues bajo ese nombre genérico se

Civil and political institutions themselves can and must be considered as veritable trials or experiments, which in the course of time reveal to us results that we could not expect, and that at times we could not even foretell. The framers of the Anglo-American constitution felt the force of these truths well, for they have always characterized it by the expressive epithet of our great experiment. Indeed, even though the political government of the United States is a republic, what points of resemblance are there between it and the republics of antiquity? What a diversity of physical, moral and political elements come into play in the one case and in the other! One need only sketch the parallel to draw the consequences. Were not all the theories of antiquity in matters of government thrown into disarray by this single example? Not because they deserve our contempt, but because, their authors not having had these new facts before their eyes, the consequent ideas could not be awakened in them. Were it otherwise, what business would be simpler than that of governing peoples? But unfortunately it is the most difficult of all, inasmuch as more than any other it demands the costly and slow fruits of experience in the moral order. Why do we hear it repeated at every step that the French revolution is the most instructive book for those who direct nations? Because it threw into disarray innumerable received doctrines, and was the fertile mother of countless others that all the perspicacity of human genius, devoted exclusively for centuries to speculating on these matters, could never have reached. We have, then, that in Ethics, in Jurisprudence, in Public Economy, in Politics, just as in any other experimental branch, facts precede enactments, experiments precede doctrines, causes precede effects: it being precisely worthy of note that when this natural method is set aside, and one tries to divine instead of hitting the mark or deducing, what is achieved is that the speculative sciences stand still and even go backward instead of ad-vancing. [p. 281] And see here precisely the fault commonly found with the ancient philosophers, who in their bold syntheses soared through imaginary fields, forgetting the firm ground of facts. How much further would the Greeks, with their brilliant gifts, not have progressed even in the experimental sciences, had they always followed this path! But once the moderns had seen the efficacy of such a method in those sciences, they could not but long—above all on perceiving the identity of origin in all of them—for its application to the sciences improperly called moral or speculative, so as to impress upon them a firmer and more rigorous course, the sure pledge of their further advancement.

And here I am naturally led to resolve another of Mr. Adicto’s doubts, concerning the backwardness in which I affirmed the moral sciences found themselves in comparison with the physical and mathematical; for as to their being sciences of observation and susceptible of progress, notwithstanding that they rest on some principles as unalterable as they are universal, not even a shadow of doubt can now remain even to the most prejudiced understanding.

Before airing this point, let Mr. Adversary permit me to remind him that under the name of moral sciences are comprised in general all those branches of human knowledge in which experiments and observations are not materially made with instruments and reagents, as is practiced in those called natural. This reminder is all the more necessary as Adicto has almost confined his argument, in order to demonstrate the perfection that in his view the moral sciences have reached, to Ethics itself and to Jurisprudence; whereas he should bear in mind that even if those two sciences were really in the state of advancement he claims, this demonstration would still not weaken in the least the general assertion that the sciences called moral are backward with respect to the natural ones, since under that generic name are

[p. 282]

> comprenden la Psicología , la Lógica , la Metafisica , la Filo-sofia de la historia , la Pedagogia la Política, la Economía pública etc ,, y como dije antes , todos aquellos ramos que si bien son de experiencia y observación , no observan y experi-mentan con aparatos é instrumentos . Por esta razón siempre me incliné á apellidar intelectuales á dichas ciencias : término sin duda menos expuesto á equívocos é interpretaciones . Así distingueremos : ciencias especulativas por excelencia , las Matemáticas , que constituyen ramo aparte ; ciencias físicas ó naturales ; y últimamente ciencias especulativas , ó intelec-tuales ó morales , que hemos ya enumerado , y participan                                      ri-gurosamente de       naturaleza de las primeras la                           segundas                    y              , bien  que aún más de estas   que    aquellas por     de ser eminen-          , temente ciencias de observación     Así    que todas puede .               es        á aplicarse este epíteto pues aún las mismas Matemáticas , tienen      su punto de partida         observación pero siendo en   la                        , las únicas que en sus progresos pueden prescindir de     ob-                             la servación quédese este distintivo como más característico ,                                                    el para las demás tocando de derecho ,                      las de la cantidad  á el de eminentemente especulativas que bajo otro sentido , intelectuales todas    son pues que en todas entra lo          ,              enten-                        el dimiento como causa        . Si   se hubiera tenido      vista esta nomenclatura que pro- á   la ponemos quizás ,             se habrían escusado muchas cuestiones cual  presente en las ciencias llamadas morales la                                       Porque                         . recordando que eran de observación ya    daba   entender          se           á que eran susceptibles de progreso   que en sus pesquisas ,    y , no debíamos atenernos exclusivamente   las deducciones de        á la razón humana      Empero .                               se reflexiona un momento ,   si conoceremos   que  en    estado en que el            hallaban los en-         se tendimientos no era tan sencillo como parece dar con una denominación que caracteriza       verdadera naturaleza de ia dichas ciencias siendo así que esa misma era ;                                 cuestión                   la              , puesto que       se estaba en    concepto de que en ellas podría el procederse meramente con       instrumento de el    razón                        la         , ó sea que las ciencias llamadas morales eran puramente cspe

comprised Psychology, Logic, Metaphysics, the Philosophy of history, Pedagogy, Politics, Public Economy, etc., and, as I said before, all those branches which, though they are of experience and observation, do not observe and experiment with apparatus and instruments. For this reason I was always inclined to call those sciences intellectual: a term doubtless less exposed to equivocations and interpretations. Thus we shall distinguish: sciences speculative par excellence, Mathematics, which constitute a separate branch; physical or natural sciences; and lastly sciences speculative, or intellectual or moral, which we have already enumerated, and which partake strictly of the nature of the first and of the second, though still more of the latter than of the former, being eminently sciences of observation. So that this epithet may be applied to all of them, for even Mathematics themselves have their starting point in observation; but, being the only ones that in their progress can dispense with observation, let this distinction remain as the most characteristic for the others, while to those of quantity belongs by right that of eminently speculative, since in another sense they are all intellectual, for in all of them the understanding enters as a cause.

Had this nomenclature that we propose been kept in view, perhaps many questions such as the present one about the sciences called moral would have been spared. For in recalling that they were sciences of observation, it was already given to understand that they were susceptible of progress, and that in their inquiries we were not to rely exclusively on the deductions of human reason. However, if we reflect a moment, we shall recognize that, in the state in which men’s understandings then were, it was not so simple as it seems to hit upon a denomination that should characterize the true nature of those sciences; since that very thing was the question, inasmuch as men were under the notion that in them one could proceed merely with the instrument of reason, or, in other words, that the sciences called moral were purely speculative.

[p. 283]

> culativas . ¡ Tan cierto es que la precisión del lenguaje vie-ne en pos de las ideas ! Hasta que los infinitos tropiezos que se daban en las ciencias morales , tanto más notables cuanto que contrastaban con la firme marcha que , gracias al método , tomaban las naturales , no desengañaron á sus cultivadores de la ineficacia de sus procedimientos , no co-menzaron á desconfiar de su razón aislada y á comprender la indispensable alianza de esta con la observación para lle-gar , y llegar bien , á la suspirada meta . Todavía no bastó que una voz tan enérgica como autorizada , al contemplar los antiguos extravios , clamase : " al entendimiento del hom-bre no conviene darle plumas para que vuele , sino plomo que le sirva de lastre . " Fué menester que los hombres vie-sen los milagros operados por estos principios en las cien-cias físicas , para que desearan aplicar tan abonado instru-mento á los otros ramos de sus investigaciones . Verdad es que no hay ramo alguno en que no partan los hombres de ciertas observaciones , así los antiguos como los modernos , pues hasta las hipótesis más atrevidas re-caen sobre hechos ú observaciones ; las ficciones mismas se inventaron no por inventarse sino para esplicar las realida-des . La diferencia , pues , entre el método puramente racio-nal y el esperimental se cifra en que el primero , creyendo suficientes para levantar el edificio de la ciencia unos es-casos datos , prescinde de ulteriores observaciones , al paso que el segundo , juzgando estas indispensables , detiene el vuelo del ingenio luego que le faltan estos preciosos esca-lones y materiales para elevar la fábrica . No de otra fuen-te nace la discordancia entre la teoría y la práctica en las ciencias intelectuales , pues cuando se aventura una doctri-na sin ir apoyada en todos los datos necesarios , como harto amenudo ha acontecido en Legislación y en Política , suele estrellarse contra los hechos no previstos , ó sean las leyes del mundo moral , que propiamente constituyen la práctica . ¿Quién no sabe que un sin número de leyes civiles de dis-tintos tiempos , no pueden ni deben considerarse sino como

How true it is that precision of language comes in the wake of ideas! Until the endless stumbles made in the moral sciences—all the more notable as they contrasted with the firm course that the natural sciences, thanks to method, were taking—undeceived their cultivators as to the inefficacy of their procedures, they did not begin to distrust their isolated reason, and to understand the indispensable alliance of reason with observation for reaching, and reaching well, the longed-for goal. It was still not enough that a voice as energetic as it was authoritative, contemplating the errors of old, should cry out: “the understanding of man must not be given feathers to fly with, but lead to serve it as ballast.” It was necessary that men should see the miracles worked by these principles in the physical sciences before they would wish to apply so well-proven an instrument to the other branches of their investigations.

It is true that there is no branch in which men do not start from certain observations, the ancients as well as the moderns, for even the boldest hypotheses bear upon facts or observations; fictions themselves were invented not for the sake of inventing, but to explain realities. The difference, then, between the purely rational method and the experimental one comes down to this, that the first, believing a few scant data sufficient to raise the edifice of science, dispenses with further observations, whereas the second, judging these indispensable, checks the flight of genius as soon as it lacks these precious steps and materials for raising the structure. From no other source springs the discord between theory and practice in the intellectual sciences; for when a doctrine is ventured without being supported by all the necessary data, as has all too often happened in Legislation and in Politics, it is wont to be dashed against unforeseen facts, that is, against the laws of the moral world, which properly constitute practice. Who does not know that a countless number of civil laws of different times cannot and must not be considered otherwise than as

[p. 284]

> verdaderos ensayos ó experimentos , que aplicados á la so-ciedad habían de revelar la acción de sus resortes , y seña-lar el camino para corregir la teoría ? Y si nos internamos en el dilatado campo de la Política , ¿quién ignora las prue-bas más ó menos funestas hechas por las naciones en su sistema de gobierno en cortísimo período ? Por do quiera que volvamos los ojos en el vasto teatro de los conocimientos humanos , hallaremos como ley inva-riable la necesidad en que está el hombre de no salir del círculo eterno de la experiencia á las analogías , y de las analogías á la experiencia , de los hechos al raciocinio y vi-ce -versa . Por lo que se vé , y dicho sea de paso , que no es nuestro ánimo rebajar en lo más leve el alto rango que ocupa la razón humana , esta centella de la Divinidad , sino al contrario , queremos hacerla más digna de su orígen , re-cordándole la ley á que la sujetó el Supremo hacedor , para asegurar el acierto que es el resultado que más puede acer-carla á él . Rigurosamente hablando no deberíamos decir que la teo-ría está en pugna con la práctica , sino más bien que es                                        in-completa    falsa ó     no abraza los hechos que comprender ,   si debe   ó  los desfigura si                 amaño pues  á    su teoría no debe,            la ser más que     expresión general la              clave que todos los ,    ó           ,        á hechos encadena      Pero no .   posible que        es razón huma-                  la na descubra desde un principio no ya los hechos todos    ,                                      , ue esos          se revelan      mismos     los revelan las circuns- á   sí la ó (q                                                       , tancias   los arranca ,   ó          ingenio      misma naturaleza pe- el             á                                  ) aun las relaciones de los hechos luego hasta en sus ro ni                                                                 : mismas teorías ha de ser forzosamente progresiva           Con                          . sobrado fundamento pues habló       que dijo que los he- ,        ,                 el chos eran más preciosos cuando contradecian que cuando confirmaban doctrinas recibidas no siendo en rigor nues- , tras teorías más que aproximaciones    conocimiento de las          al cosas  . veritable trials or experiments which, applied to society, were to reveal the action of its springs and point out the way to correct the theory? And if we go into the wide field of Politics, who is unaware of the more or less disastrous trials made by nations in their system of government within a very brief period?

Wherever we turn our eyes in the vast theater of human knowledge, we shall find as an invariable law the necessity under which man lies of not leaving the eternal circle from experience to analogies, and from analogies to experience, from facts to reasoning, and vice versa. From which it is seen—and be it said in passing— that it is not our intention to lower in the slightest the high rank that human reason occupies, this spark of the Divinity; on the contrary, we wish to make it more worthy of its origin, by reminding it of the law to which the Supreme Maker subjected it, in order to ensure that sureness of aim which is the result that can bring it nearest to Him.

Strictly speaking, we ought not to say that theory is at odds with practice, but rather that it is incomplete or false, if it does not embrace the facts it ought to comprehend, or if it distorts them to suit itself; for theory must be no more than the general expression, or key, that links all the facts together. But it is not possible for human reason to discover from the outset, not merely all the facts (for these reveal themselves, or circumstances reveal them, or genius wrests them from nature herself), but not even the relations of the facts: hence even in its very theories it must necessarily be progressive. With ample grounds, then, did he speak who said that facts were more precious when they contradicted received doctrines than when they confirmed them, our theories being, strictly, no more than approximations to the knowledge of things.

Before entering upon the comparison of some sciences with others, allow me, for the sake of greater clarity, to point out:

[p. 285]

> 1. Hay ciertos principios en las morales tan evidentes y seguros como los que rigen en las matemáticas ; v . g . , está tan demostrada la existencia del pensamiento como cual-quier   axioma de geometría , y tan patente que la salud es -un bien y la enfermedad un mal come que dos y dos son cuatro . 2 . De aquí no se infiere que en lo demás sean dichas ciencias del mismo rigor que las matemáticas . 3 . - Recuérdese que en estas puede continuarse con solo el ra- -ciocinio , al paso que en las otras ciencias no es posible sin la observación . 4. Esta suele ser más fácil y prontamen-te realizable en las experimentales que en las morales.- 5. El instrumento del cálculo , aunque aplicable á todas hasta cierto punto , lo es más á las primeras que á las se-gundas , y así se esplica el admirable estado de adelanto à que han llegado muchos ramos de la Física . Todo esto presupuesto , entremos más de lleno en la cues-tión . Y empezando el cotejo por la Psicología , solo el hecho de la diversa solución que se ha dado á la del orígen de las ideas , cuestión que encontramos propuesta desde los pri-meros pasos de la ciencia , bastaría para decidir la que tan-to nos ocupa . Tomémosla tan solo desde la antígua Grecia , y desde luego advertiremos cuan diversamente la resolvie-ron Platón y Aristóteles . Siguieron divididas siglos y mas siglos las escuelas formadas por estos insignes caudillos en cuestión tan fundamental en la ciencia , que por sí sola basta á caracterizar y aún á producir la diversidad entre los sis-temas filosóficos . Reinó después , casi exclusivamente , la solución del Estagirita durante el largo periodo del esco-lasticismo , hasta que viniendo al mundo el grau Descartes y derrocando el peripato , revivió y modificó las ideas de Pla-tón . Preséntase después Locke en Inglaterra reproducien-do con nuevos datos el sistema sensualista , y á poco apare-ce en Alemania una estrella de primera magnitud , el uni-versal Leibnitz , que trata de alumbrar y alumbra todos los horizontes de la ciencia , y pretendiendo conciliar el sensua-lismo con el espiritualismo ( lo que en sí ya es otra solución )

1st. There are certain principles in the moral sciences as evident and certain as those that hold in mathematics; for instance, the existence of thought is as demonstrated as any axiom of geometry, and it is as patent that health is a good and sickness an evil as that two and two make four.—2nd. It does not follow from this that in the rest these sciences are of the same rigor as mathematics.—3rd. Let it be remembered that in mathematics one can proceed with reasoning alone, whereas in the other sciences this is not possible without observation.—4th. Observation is usually more easily and promptly carried out in the experimental sciences than in the moral.—5th. The instrument of calculation, though applicable to all up to a certain point, is more so to the former than to the latter; and thus is explained the admirable state of advancement that many branches of Physics have reached.

All this presupposed, let us enter more fully into the question. And beginning the comparison with Psychology, the mere fact of the diverse solutions that have been given to the question of the origin of ideas—a question we find proposed from the very first steps of the science—would suffice to decide the one that occupies us so much. Let us take it only from ancient Greece, and we shall at once notice how differently Plato and Aristotle resolved it. For centuries upon centuries the schools formed by these illustrious leaders remained divided upon a question so fundamental in the science, that by itself alone it is enough to characterize, and even to produce, the diversity among philosophical systems. Thereafter, almost exclusively, the solution of the Stagirite reigned during the long period of scholasticism, until the great Descartes came into the world and, overthrowing the Peripatetic school, revived and modified the ideas of Plato. Then Locke appears in England, reproducing with new data the sensationalist system, and shortly afterwards there appears in Germany a star of the first magnitude, the universal Leibniz, who tries to illuminate, and does illuminate, all the horizons of science, and, claiming to reconcile sensationalism with spiritualism (which is in itself already another solution),

[p. 286]

> confiesa francamente la tendencia de sus opiniones mas bien hácia las del idealista griego que á las de su esclarecido discípulo . Pero á pesar de este impulso dado por Leibnitz á la Filosofía , hace sin embargo fortuna en Francia el sensualis-mo en manos de Condillac y de la famosa escuela que le siguió , á là sazón que en el Norte de Alemania se presentaba otro gran pensador original , Kant , llamando á examen las opiniones dominantes , y produciendo una revolución en los espíritus , la más notable quizás después de Cartesio , aunque por en-tonces confinada todavía á los límites de la dilatada famiiia teutónica : revolución que volvía á llamarlos al espiritualis-mo , pero á un espiritualismo muy modificado , pues Kant no es rigurosamente platónico ni cartesiano . Por el mismo tiempo comenzaba á florecer en Escocia la famosa escuela de Edimburgo , que inclinándose al espiritualismo , fincó sin embargo su mayor empeño en hacer una historia completa de los fenómenos del alma , para preparar una teoría de sus facultades , que todavía se deja desear en la ciencia . No ha-blaré de los sistemas y variedades de sistemas en que se di-vidió y subdividió la Alemania después de Kant: bastaráme citar los nombres mas notables de Fichte , Jacobi , Herder , Hegel , Schelling y Gruppe , con que llegamos hasta nuestros días ; y volviendo los ojos hácia la Francia moderna , donde había el sensualismo echado tan hondas raices , gracias á la filosofía del siglo XVIII no ménos que á los progresos de la escuela fisiológica , encontraremos al famoso Cousin , ( 1 ) importando y queriendo aclimatar en su patria el nuevo idealismo alemán , á quien había preparado el camino por medio de las doctrinas escocesas , mas relacionadas con aquel sistema , el célebre Royer Collard . Mas apenas se pre-sentan estos campeones en la arena , cuando otros adalides no ménos esforzados salen á disputarles el terreno , y á des-cargarles golpes de que no es fácil levantarse . (1) Cousin es discípulo de Hegel y Schelling , pero en cuanto á su plan de conciliación ó su eclecticismo , como él lo entiende , es propia-mente alumno de Leibnitz .

frankly confesses the leaning of his opinions toward those of the Greek idealist rather than toward those of his illustrious disciple. But in spite of this impulse given by Leibniz to Philosophy, sensationalism nevertheless makes its fortune in France in the hands of Condillac and of the famous school that followed him, at the very time when in the North of Germany there appeared another great original thinker, Kant, summoning the dominant opinions to examination and producing a revolution in men’s minds, perhaps the most notable since Descartes, though at that time still confined within the limits of the wide Teutonic family: a revolution that called them back to spiritualism, but to a much modified spiritualism, for Kant is not strictly Platonic nor Cartesian.—About the same time there began to flourish in Scotland the famous school of Edinburgh, which, though inclining to spiritualism, nevertheless placed its chief endeavor in making a complete history of the phenomena of the soul, in order to prepare a theory of its faculties, which is still wanting in the science. I shall not speak of the systems and varieties of systems into which Germany divided and subdivided itself after Kant: it will suffice me to cite the most notable names of Fichte, Jacobi, Herder, Hegel, Schelling and Gruppe, with which we come down to our own days; and turning our eyes toward modern France, where sensationalism had struck such deep roots, thanks to the philosophy of the eighteenth century no less than to the progress of the physiological school, we shall find the famous Cousin, (1) importing and seeking to acclimatize in his country the new German idealism, for which the celebrated Royer-Collard had prepared the way by means of the Scottish doctrines, more closely related to that system. But scarcely do these champions present themselves in the arena when other captains, no less valiant, come out to dispute the ground with them and to deal them blows from which it is not easy to rise.

(1) Cousin is a disciple of Hegel and Schelling, but as regards his plan of conciliation, or his eclecticism as he understands it, he is properly a pupil of Leibniz.

[p. 287]

> Esta imperfectísima reseña histórica , es más que sufi-ciente para mi propósito , reducido á demostrar el atraso respectivo de la Psicología , por las vicisitudes de las opi- -niones en la cuestión fundamental del orígen de las ideas , tan antígua como la ciencia .
