## P hilosophy . (1)

Correction.

To the Citizen of the world, residing in Trinidad, greetings!

Great is the honor you do Mr. Varela and me in pointing out that, notwithstanding our intimate friendship, we differ in philosophical opinions. But this proposition, presented thus in isolation, and above all conceived in the terms in which you have put it, deserves more than one correction. —Here are the words of the “Citizen of the world:” “Even Don José de la Luz y Caballero, who, according to what I hear, is perhaps a greater friend of Mr. Varela than you (the Lugareño) are, does not follow his philosophy.” “Evident proof,

Don José Ignacio Rodríguez reproduced this piece by Luz in Appendix E of his “Vida del Presbítero D. Félix Varela.—Nueva-York—1878.”—(A. Z.)

(a) See Appendix no. 17.—(A. Z.)

(1) I insert this article immediately after the polemics on Question of Method, because of its reference to them. It was published in the “Gaceta de Puerto Príncipe” of May 2, 1840, preceded by the following lines from Don Anastasio de Orozco.—“Mr. Editor of the ‘Gaceta de Puerto del Príncipe.’ Dear Sir: I send you an article which my very dear friend and kinsman Don José de la Luz y Caballero has sent me from Havana; he forgoes the pleasure of publishing it in that city for the friendly sentiment of defending our friend Lugareño on his own ground, Camagüey, where the question with the Citizen of the world has been raised.” (a)

[p. 344]

> añade V. llevando demasiado lejos la consecuencia        de su misma premisa , de que no está acorde ni con su método , ni con sus doctrinas filosóficas " Dije que los asertos de V. habían menester más de una rectificación , y lo pruebo al punto . Desde luego , no por discrepar yo en algunas pocas opi- niones de las del Señor Varela , puede asentarse con funda- mento que yo no sigo su filosofia , palabra bajo la cual se en- cierra todo un sistema de doctrinas . Sabido es que la .... obra de mi ilustre paisano sirve de texto á mis lecciones en todos los días de la semana escepto el sábado , y á veces otro más , que consagro exclusivamente á la impugnación de las doctrinas de la escuela ecléctica francesa , valiéndo- me de los mismos escritos de su famoso corifeo para blan- co de nuestra polémica . Y vea V. ahora brevemente , Sr Ciudadano del mundo , como soy discipulo de Varela bajo muchos aspectos . Vare- la derrocó el escolasticismo en nuestro suelo , y yo aplau- do y aplaudiré su ruina . Varela fué nuestro legítimo Car- tesio , en más de un sentido , ya por haber destruído el principio de autoridad con el consejo y el ejemplo de pala- bra y obra , ya por haber introducido en su consecuencia la libertad filosófica de pensar , el verdadero eclecticismo ; asi es que , no contento con destruir , se empeñó en edificar , y edificar con los materiales de la mas esquisita calidad que tuviera a su disposición ; precisamente con los que sir- ven hoy de base hasta á aquellas de mis doctrinas en que *discrepamos , o podemos discrepar .    Varela dió el grande , el atrevido paso de introducir la Fisiología , elemento indis- pensable para el estudio completo del hombre , en el cam- po de la ciencia .     Yo , no como quiera , sigo en esto sus huellas , sino que veo en aquel estudio el porvenir no sólo de la Filosofía estrictamente tal , sino hasta de la Educa- ción , la Moral , y la Legislación . Varela fué siempre enemigo declarado de toda Ontología , y yo no ceso de hacerle la guerra á ese Proteo , sean como

you add, carrying the consequence of your own premise too far, that he is in accord neither with his method nor with his philosophical doctrines.” I said that your assertions stood in need of more than one correction, and I shall prove it at once.

To begin with, it cannot be asserted with any foundation, merely because I disagree with some few of Mr. Varela’s opinions, that I do not follow his philosophy, a word under which a whole system of doctrines is comprised. It is well known that the work of my illustrious countryman serves as the text for my lessons on every day of the week except Saturday, and sometimes one day more, which I devote exclusively to refuting the doctrines of the French eclectic school, making the very writings of its famous coryphaeus the target of our polemic.

And see now, briefly, Mr. Citizen of the world, how I am a disciple of Varela in many respects. Varela overthrew scholasticism on our soil, and I applaud and shall applaud its ruin. Varela was our legitimate Descartes, in more than one sense: both for having destroyed the principle of authority by counsel and example, in word and deed, and for having in consequence introduced philosophical freedom of thought, the true eclecticism; so that, not content with destroying, he set himself to build, and to build with materials of the most exquisite quality he had at his disposal; precisely with those which serve today as the basis even of those of my doctrines in which we differ, or may differ. Varela took the great, the bold step of introducing Physiology, an indispensable element for the complete study of man, into the field of science. I do not merely follow in his footsteps in this, but see in that study the future not only of Philosophy strictly so called, but even of Education, Ethics, and Legislation.

Varela was always the declared enemy of all Ontology, and I never cease to wage war on that Proteus, whatever

[p. 345]

> fueren las formas especiosas , y aún venerandas bajo las cuales procura presentarse .. Varela , columbró primero y mas que nadie en este país , la importancia de las ciencias físicas , no ya solo para los adelantamientos materiales de la sociedad , sino para dirigir y robustecer al entendimiento en todo género de investiga-ciones y muy particularmente para el progreso de la Filoso-fía racional , ó propiamente dicha .    Yo tengo por escusado demostrar que abundo en semejantes principios por ser noto-rios mis conatos por la difusión de este género de conocimien-tos , que hacen falta en todas carreras y circunstancias , y muy especialmente á una gran parte de nuestra juventud que , dedicada exclusivamente á la Jurisprudencia , carece de cri-terio para juzgar de infinitos casos que se le presentan des-pués en el vastísimo campo de las transacciones humanas ; esta falta es también causa muy principal de que cundan en-tre nosotros muchos de los errores de que están plagadas las -obras de los metafísicos , y señaladamente de los nuevos pseudo eclecticos , inclusos los mismos que son fisiolo-gístas de la escuela . Por último , y por no prolongar más esta reseña , Varela , no satisfecho con emancipar nuestro entendimiento , no sa-tisfecho con lo que parecía sustancial , queriendo hacer la reforma efectiva se ocupó también del instrumento yama-nera de Julio César nihil actum reputans , si quid superes-set agendum cortó también las trabas que encadenaban la exposición de las ciencias á los signos de una lengua muerta , aunque idolatrada y poseída por él (más mérito !) en un grado de que todavía no pueden formar idea los que sólo juzguen por sus escritos en aquel idioma divino á pesar de la elegancia y aticismo que los distingue : pues para gra-duar su fuerza era necesario haber experimentado en el dulce comercio con este dulcísimo Varela la soltura y faci-lidad con que manejaba en la conversación familiar la lengua de Marco Tulio y de Terencio . Yo aunque tan afi-cionado como él , y como el que más , á la lengua robusta

the specious, and even venerable, forms in which it seeks to present itself.

Varela was the first, and more than anyone in this country, to discern the importance of the physical sciences, not only for the material advancement of society, but for directing and strengthening the understanding in every kind of investigation, and very particularly for the progress of rational Philosophy, or Philosophy properly so called. I hold it superfluous to demonstrate that I abound in the same principles, my endeavors for the diffusion of this kind of knowledge being notorious—knowledge that is wanted in all careers and circumstances, and very especially by a great part of our youth, who, devoted exclusively to Jurisprudence, lack a criterion for judging the countless cases that later present themselves to them in the vast field of human transactions; this want is also a very principal cause of the spread among us of many of the errors with which the works of the metaphysicians are infested, and notably those of the new pseudo-eclectics, not excepting even those who are physiologists of the school.

Lastly, and not to prolong this review further, Varela, not satisfied with emancipating our understanding, not satisfied with what seemed the substance, and wishing to make the reform effective, attended also to the instrument, and in the manner of Julius Caesar, nihil actum reputans, si quid superesset agendum [counting nothing done while anything remained to be done], he cut as well the shackles that chained the exposition of the sciences to the signs of a dead language, though one idolized and possessed by him (the greater merit!) to a degree of which those who judge only by his writings in that divine idiom, despite the elegance and Atticism that distinguish them, can as yet form no idea: for to gauge his mastery one had to have experienced, in sweet intercourse with this sweetest Varela, the ease and facility with which he handled the tongue of Marcus Tullius and of Terence in familiar conversation. I, though as fond as he, and as fond as any man, of the robust tongue

[p. 346]

> del Lacio , á esa lengua de hombres que eran hombres , no he menester decir ( ¿y quién puede ya poner en duda seme-jante principio mediando el siglo XIX ? ) que sacrificaría to-das mis aficiones en gracia de proporcionar el vehículo más facil y expeditivo para la difusión de los conocimientos . Y   con esto me parece sobradamente rectificado el primer aserto del Sr. Ciudadano del mundo       Pasemos ahora á la otra rectificación prometida : " Prueba evidente , añade V. de que no está acorde ( el que esto escribe ) ni con su método , ni con sus doctrinas . " En primer lugar , tacho la consecuencia , pues de que difieran dos indivíduos en algunas , y hasta en muchas opiniones , en el vasto campo de una ciencia y sobre todo en la ciencia de las ciencias , no se infiere en buena lógica que discrepen hasta en el método , y tan no hay repugnancia , que aún en las ciencias de peculiar experimentación , v . g . en la Quími-ca , siguiendo todos sus cultivadores el mismo método de apelar al laboratorio y aun obteniendo á veces los mismos hechos , se suscitan las más acaloradas controversias acer-ca de las inducciones que de los mencionados datos quie-ren sacarse , toda vez que esa operación es obra de la cabe-za de cada uno , y ha lugar por lo mismo al tot capita tot setentiæ : testigo las empeñadísimas contiendas que me-dian hoy mismo entre el famoso químico sueco Berzelius y uno de los primeros de Francia que es Dumas . En segundo lugar , muy probable es se haya figurado el Sr. Ciudadano del mundo , que por colocar el Sr. Varela su Lógica y Moral antes de la Física , en sus " Lecciones de Fi-losofía " y haber yo sostenido , y á mi parecer probado , que las ciencias físicas deben estudiarse previa ó independiente . mente de las llamadas morales , difiramos completamente en la cuestión de método , ú orden , en la enseñanza .Ya fé que en esta parte ha tenido motivos para juzgar así el señor Ciudadano , que no encontrará en mi más que justicia é imparcialidad . Pero voy á exponer con brevedad lo que media en el particular , y espero dejar completamente satis-

of Latium, that tongue of men who were men, need not say (and who can any longer call such a principle into question in the middle of the XIXth century?) that I would sacrifice all my predilections for the sake of providing the easiest and most expeditious vehicle for the diffusion of knowledge.

And with this the first assertion of Mr. Citizen of the world seems to me more than sufficiently corrected. Let us pass now to the other correction promised:

“Evident proof, you add, that he (the present writer) is in accord neither with his method nor with his doctrines.” In the first place, I object to the inference; for from the fact that two individuals differ in some, and even in many, opinions in the vast field of a science, and above all in the science of sciences, it does not follow in good logic that they disagree even in method; and so far is there from being any contradiction in this, that even in the sciences of peculiar experimentation, for example in Chemistry, though all its cultivators follow the same method of appealing to the laboratory, and even at times obtain the same facts, the most heated controversies arise over the inductions that are sought to be drawn from the said data, since that operation is the work of each man’s head, and there is therefore room for the tot capita tot sententiæ [so many heads, so many opinions]: witness the hard-fought contests going on at this very day between the famous Swedish chemist Berzelius and one of the foremost chemists of France, namely Dumas.

In the second place, it is very probable that Mr. Citizen of the world has imagined that, because Mr. Varela places his Logic and Ethics before Physics in his “Lecciones de Filosofía,” and because I have maintained, and in my view proved, that the physical sciences ought to be studied before, or independently of, the so-called moral sciences, we differ completely on the question of method, or order, in teaching. And in good faith Mr. Citizen has had grounds for judging thus on this point, for he will find in me nothing but justice and impartiality. But I shall set forth briefly how the matter stands, and I hope to leave completely satisfied

[p. 347]

> fecho mi propósito de rectificar       el referido segundo con-cepto . Bien podría ser que el Sr. Varela no estuviese en aquella época (hace más de veinte años ) en mis ideas acerca de la cuestión de método ; pero aunque lo estuviere no se hallaba en su mano exclusivamente alterar el órden general de los estudios en aquel tiempo , así en el mismo Seminario de San Cárlos , como en la Real y Pontificia Universidad de quien pendía y pende ese establecimiento . ( 1 ) Verdad es que los Estatutos del Colegio daban mucha más amplitud que los de la Universidad al profesor para hacer alteraciones y me-joras , y nuestro patriótico y celoso maestro se aprovechó de tan preciosa circunstancia para realizar cuantas refor-mas pudo en obsequio de la juventud estudiosa del país . ¡ Qué más !  Traspasólos límites del estatuto en más de una reforma importantísima y trascendental , como queda pro-bado , luchando y siempre luchando , que nada grande se consigue sin lucha , y apoyado á veces por las insinuaciones y consejos del grande Espada ( unicuique suum ) cabeza suprema del Seminario y cabeza nacida para todo . Diversas , empero , han sido las circunstancias en que yo me he encontrado respecto á la cuestión de órden en los estudios . Puede decirse con verdad que no he tenido sino querer y lograr . Tratábase efectivamente de establecer cá-tedras de Filosofía en los colegios de San Fernando y San Cristóbal , por los años de 1833 , y como por la Real dispo-sición del caso se cometiese al siempre lamentado D. Fran-cisco Arango y Parreño , á título de comisionado especial para el plan de estudios , la inspección y sanción interina de cuanto propusiesen al intento los Directores de di-chos establecimientos , que lo eran á la sazón D. Narciso Piñeyro del primero y el que habla del segundo , aprove- (1) Hoy mismo el Sr. Ruiz que profesa en el Seminario y en Carra-guao , principia el curso en el primer establecimiento por la Lógica y en el segundo por la Física .

my purpose of correcting the said second notion.

It may well be that Mr. Varela did not at that period (more than twenty years ago) share my ideas on the question of method; but even had he shared them, it was not exclusively in his power to alter the general order of studies at that time, either in the San Carlos Seminary itself or in the Royal and Pontifical University, on which that establishment depended and still depends. (1) It is true that the Statutes of the College allowed the professor much more latitude than those of the University for making alterations and improvements, and our patriotic and zealous master took advantage of so precious a circumstance to carry out as many reforms as he could for the benefit of the studious youth of the country. What is more! He overstepped the limits of the statute in more than one most important and far-reaching reform, as has been proved, struggling and ever struggling—for nothing great is achieved without struggle— and supported at times by the suggestions and counsels of the great Espada (unicuique suum [to each his own]), supreme head of the Seminary and a head born for everything.

Different, however, have been the circumstances in which I have found myself with respect to the question of order in studies. It may truly be said that for me it has been only to wish and to obtain. It was in fact a matter of establishing chairs of Philosophy in the colleges of San Fernando and San Cristóbal, about the year 1833, and as the Royal order on the matter entrusted to the ever-lamented Don Francisco Arango y Parreño, in the capacity of special commissioner for the plan of studies, the inspection and interim sanction of whatever the Directors of the said establishments might propose to that end—these being at the time Don Narciso Piñeyro of the first and the present speaker of the second—we seized

the opportunity to promote all the improvements and reforms we judged useful, and among them the precedence, not preference, of the study of Physics in the course of Philosophy, according to the branches of which it consists on our soil; and we seized the opportunity with all the more spirit since we were sure of the approval of the enlightened Mr. Arango for whatever redounded to the benefit of the country, the unceasing object of his vigilance throughout his long public career. The said improvement had the good fortune to obtain, not merely his approval, but his most decided applause, as no one is unaware at present, least of all in Puerto Príncipe, after the polemic raised there at the beginning of 1838 by Mr. Rumilio, and continued by the Dómine in the same Gaceta of Camagüey, with him who traces these rough lines.

But be that as it may, let Mr. Citizen of the world know that I have the honor of counting Mr. Varela among the decided partisans of the method of teaching Physics before Psychology, as he has expressly declared to me in a letter written months ago from New York, (1) which I do not have before me now; and, to be more precise, he adds in it, if my memory is not unfaithful, that he was in everything of my opinion, and perhaps also for other reasons which I had not adduced, or something to that effect, for I remember the spirit more than the letter.

So then, believing that I have fulfilled my purpose of correcting the mistaken notion under which Mr. Citizen of the World labors regarding my philosophical opinions as compared with those of my illustrious master, I conclude by hoping from his sense of justice that he will be pleased to apply to the case the precious maxim so opportunely invoked by El Lugareño, by that patriot proof against every test, who is all chivalry and good intention, sapientis est mutare consilium [it is the part of a wise man to change his counsel]; and let the Citizen know, and let the world know, that the modest Lugareño, in rendering that

> testimonio de su celo al esclarecido Varela , no hizo más que ceder á un sentimiento profundo de gratitud , de justi-cia , de amor á su suelo , pués mientras se piense en la Isla de Cuba , se pensará en quien nos enseñó primero á pensar . Habana 20 de Abril de 1840 .

testimony of his zeal to the illustrious Varela, did nothing but yield to a profound feeling of gratitude, of justice, of love for his native soil; for so long as the Island of Cuba is thought of, he will be thought of who first taught us to think.

Havana, April 20, 1840.

## P hilosophy . (1)

On reading the discussion that has arisen over an article written by M. Costales on the necessity of the study of Ideology for that of Literature, and criticized with excessive levity and injustice by an Eclectic, who suddenly and without previous recommendations has appeared for the first time before the public with the vain and pompous title of Savior of Philosophy, we have taken up the pen to make various observations, which have no other object than to prove the falsity of some doctrines which Mr. Eclectic blindly adopts and follows, and the great errors he has committed through having disregarded the rules of ideology in setting up a purely literary discussion. We shall say nothing of the spirit of opposition observable in his writings, because in taking that trouble we should be false to our character, and it would appear clearly

The discussion once begun, Costales maintained his opinions in the Diarios of August 16 and September 13, and “The Eclectic” his in those of August 24 and September 27.— (A. Z.)

Sí el Sr. Ecléctico , guiado por la luz de la razón , se hu-biese atenido tan solo á los hechos , hubiera abierto una discusión del más alto interés para las ciencias ; pero incau-to , ó tal vez mal aconsejado , prefirió lanzarse en el abismo de las conjeturas ; y como el Sr. Ecléctico , según se deduce de sus escritos , no está muy acostumbrado á la exactitud en sus juicios , ni se detiene mucho en sacar consecuencias , ni observa en fin las reglas filosóficas mejor demostradas al entrar en una cuestión , y declarándole una oposición siste-mática á la escuela de Condillac desprecia hasta la palabra ideologia como propia del siglo                      XVIII , ha caido inevitable y forzosamente en el error, dando pruebas con esto de que está muy poco instruido en materias filosóficas , y que no ha sabido sostener el título pomposo de Salvador de la Filosofía con que el mismo se ha regalado . proved before the public that Mr. Savior of Philosophy has not been able to be the savior of himself, because, giving entry to the passions, he has directed his ill-advised pen along a path contrary to the one he ought to have followed as a teacher of youth and as Savior of Philosophy.

If Mr. Eclectic, guided by the light of reason, had kept solely to the facts, he would have opened a discussion of the highest interest for the sciences; but, incautious, or perhaps ill-advised, he preferred to hurl himself into the abyss of conjectures; and as Mr. Eclectic, as may be deduced from his writings, is not much accustomed to exactness in his judgments, nor dwells much on drawing consequences, nor observes, in short, the best-demonstrated philosophical rules on entering upon a question, and, declaring a systematic opposition to the school of Condillac, scorns even the word ideology as belonging to the XVIIIth century, he has inevitably and necessarily fallen into error, thereby giving proof that he is very little instructed in philosophical matters, and that he has not known how to sustain the pompous title of Savior of Philosophy with which he has presented himself.

When a man filled with an investigating and philosophical spirit seeks the truth, animated solely by the desire to find it; when a well-understood wish to diffuse enlightenment brings his writings before a public in which he may perhaps meet learned and profound philosophers who will judge them severely, he ought to proceed with great moderation, arguing only with the weapons of reason and of conviction, without ungratefully insulting the memory of celebrated men who have rendered great services to the sciences, without despising their opinions merely because they belonged to past centuries. Let these be examined with deliberation and impartiality, let them be combated with reasons, not with sophisms, and if they were generally adopted, and it is proved that they are erroneous and that by their interest and high importance they compromise society and stand opposed to the progress of enlightenment, then, and only then, could

[p. 353]

> driamos nosotros decir al que prestara servicio tan grande : V. ha sido útil á la juventud de nuestra patria y al mundo entero ; V. merece nuestra gratitud y nuestra admiración por haber sido nuestro Salvador . Decir que la Ideología es la divisa de la escuela del sen-sualismo , es no entender el verdadero significado de esta palabra ; es hacer interpretaciones arbitrarias incompatibles con la rectitud conque debe siempre proceder un buen filó-sofo . Sepa V. Sr. Ecléctico que la palabra ideología quiere decir : aquella parte de la filosofía que trata del orígen de nuestras ideas . Con ella no se especifica el medio como se adquieren , pues este conocimiento es el resultado de su es-tudio . Dice el Sr. Ecléctico con mucha ligereza que el señor Costales no debió usar la palabra ideología porque es ense-ña del siglo XVIII ; esto prueba hasta la evidencia que el Sr. Ecléctico no estudia el origen de nuestras ideas , ó lo que es lo mismo no estudia ideologia , y como este estudio cons-tituye el objeto de la escuela de Condillac , se deduce nece-sariamente que el es enemigo mortal de esta escucla ; luego el que se firma Eciéctico no es ecléctico , sino un sistemático , acérrimo defensor del espiritualismo ; luego no es el de-seo de propagar la ilustración       el que mueve su plu-ma . El Sr. Sistemático , pues así lo llamaremos de aquí en ade-lante , admite ciegamente que las abstracciones son ideas ; él no ha fijado el sentido verdadero de esta palabra , y senti-mos decirle que en esto ha cometido un grave error , pues siendo la abstracción la consideración de una propiedad co-mo existente por sí sola , es una operación del alma ; á menos que el Sr. Sistemático no haya variado la significación de esta palabra acomodándola á su sistema , ó quiera , como una consecuencia precisa de sus principios , confundir los medios de adquirir las ideas con las ideas mismas . El Sr. Sistemático afirma ciegamente que en nada se dife-rencia la historia de las ciencias de la del género humano ; sen-timos también decirle que en esto comete otro grave error , 23

we say to him who should render so great a service: You have been useful to the youth of our country and to the whole world; you deserve our gratitude and our admiration for having been our Savior.

To say that Ideology is the badge of the school of sensationalism is not to understand the true meaning of this word; it is to make arbitrary interpretations incompatible with the rectitude with which a good philosopher ought always to proceed. Know, Mr. Eclectic, that the word ideology means: that part of philosophy which treats of the origin of our ideas. It does not specify the means by which they are acquired, for that knowledge is the result of its study. Mr. Eclectic says with great levity that Mr. Costales ought not to have used the word ideology because it is the ensign of the XVIIIth century; this proves to the point of evidence that Mr. Eclectic does not study the origin of our ideas, or, what is the same, does not study ideology; and as this study constitutes the object of the school of Condillac, it follows necessarily that he is the mortal enemy of that school; therefore he who signs himself Eclectic is no eclectic, but a systematist, a most stubborn defender of spiritualism; therefore it is not the desire to propagate enlightenment that moves his pen.

Mr. Systematist, for so we shall call him henceforth, blindly admits that abstractions are ideas; he has not fixed the true sense of this word, and we regret to tell him that in this he has committed a grave error, for abstraction, being the consideration of a property as existing by itself alone, is an operation of the soul; unless Mr. Systematist has altered the meaning of this word, accommodating it to his system, or wishes, as a necessary consequence of his principles, to confound the means of acquiring ideas with the ideas themselves.

Mr. Systematist blindly affirms that the history of the sciences in no way differs from that of the human race; we regret also to tell him that in this he commits another grave error,

[p. 354]

> pues siendo las ciencias un conjunto de principios      exactos , los errores solo pertenecen                  y á su historia ; como la del gé-nero humano    comprende    los vicios , crímenes , delitos etc. de  los hombres  es claro y evidente que no entra en el domi-nio de las ciencias . Luego en mucho se diferencia la histo-ria de las ciencias de la del género humano , luego el señor Sistemático no ha comprendido lo que sobre esto le ha di-cho el Sr. M. Costales , ó es tenaz y rebelde á la fuerza de la razón y á las convicciones del raciocinio . La exactitud en las ideas ; he aquí el principal mérito del historiador y del filósofo . Sin este requisito esencial nin-gun valor tendrían sus producciones , y lejos de interesarnos en su favor las miraríamos con indiferencia y desagrado , la-mentando sus desaciertos y errores . Esto nismo decimos del poeta , pues siendo las palabras la expresión de nuestras ideas , si aquellas no son exactas tampoco lo serán estas . Cuando los poetas no expresan con exactitud sus ideas , los consideramos como ilusos y á sus producciones partos de una imaginación delirante , y lamentamos sus extravíos . El verdadero filósofo busca siempre la exactitud y la ver-dad , combatiendo el error donde quiera que se encuentre , donde quiera que lo proteja el amor propio , y como el señor Sistemático sostiene ciegamente que para ser poeta es nece-sario ser inexacto , ó lo que es lo mismo cometer errores , sacamos en consecuencia que el Sr. Sistemático es anti-filosófico , y siéndolo no lo consideramos como hombre que busca imparcialmente la verdad . Así pues , no debió dispu-tar de materias filosóficas , y él es el que ataca y amenaza el estado actual de la filosofia proclamando errores y soste-niendo falsas doctrinas , El Sr. Sistemático afirma que la Ideología " es enseña del siglo   XVIII ; " este es otro error, pues en el siglo que al-canzamos se ha recomendado y recomienda el estudio de nuestras primitivas ideas , que debe necesariamente pre-ceder al de las ideas posteriores , al de esas ideas abstrac-tas que el hombre no forma sino cuando está acostum

for, the sciences being a body of exact principles, errors belong only to their history; and as that of the human race comprises the vices, crimes, offenses, etc. of men, it is clear and evident that it does not enter into the domain of the sciences. Therefore the history of the sciences differs much from that of the human race; therefore Mr. Systematist has not understood what Mr. M. Costales has told him on this point, or else he is stubborn and rebellious against the force of reason and the convictions of reasoning.

The exactness of ideas: here is the principal merit of the historian and of the philosopher. Without this essential requisite their productions would have no value, and far from interesting us in their favor, we should regard them with indifference and displeasure, lamenting their blunders and errors. The same we say of the poet, for, words being the expression of our ideas, if the former are not exact, neither will the latter be. When poets do not express their ideas with exactness, we consider them deluded, and their productions the offspring of a delirious imagination, and we lament their aberrations. The true philosopher always seeks exactness and truth, combating error wherever it may be found, wherever self-love may protect it; and as Mr. Systematist blindly maintains that to be a poet it is necessary to be inexact, or, what is the same, to commit errors, we conclude that Mr. Systematist is anti-philosophical, and, he being so, we do not regard him as a man who seeks the truth impartially. Thus, then, he ought not to have disputed on philosophical matters, and it is he who attacks and threatens the present state of philosophy, proclaiming errors and upholding false doctrines.

Mr. Systematist affirms that Ideology “is the ensign of the XVIIIth century;” this is another error, for in the century we have reached the study of our primitive ideas has been and is recommended, a study which must necessarily precede that of later ideas, of those abstract ideas which man does not form until he is accustomed

[p. 355]

> brado á pensar .    El articulista dice en el párrafo 7º de su estreno público que " la Psicología es el estudio de las ideas ," y expresándose así de un modo tan general y vago , debe forzosamente convenir en que para este estudio procede empezar por el origen de nuestras ideas , de aquellas que primero se adquieren , y seguir el desarrollo gradual de las otras ideas , para tener un conocimiento completo y exacto de ellas . Estas y no otras son las reglas prescritas por una filosofía verdadera y luminosa , y que debe seguir el que se dedica al estudio de las ciencias . El que prescinda de esta base fundamental de conocimientos posteriores , á cada pa-so tropezará con el error , no sabrá sostener la verdad , y sus escritos llevarán un sello de torpeza y de inexactitud . Lue-go el estudio de la Ideología es necesario para el de la Lite-ratura , luego nada ha probado el Sr. Sistemático con sus artículos . Concluiremos observando que en el artículo " Ideología ," nada se dice de sensualismo , nada de espiritualismo ; que no hay en él una idea siquiera , una opinión , por donde sospe-charse pueda la escuela á que pertenece su autor . Este al escribirlo trató de alentar á la juventud de nuestra patria , para que procediendo siempre con arreglo á los principios ideológicos , pensara con exactitud , y haciendo sus produc-ciones dignas del aprecio y consideración de los hombres sensatos , contribuyeran de este modo á los adelantos de las ciencias y á los progresos de la ilustración . Nosotros esta-mos persuadidos de que si este mismo artículo , que tan amargamente ha criticado el Sr. Sistemático , hubiese lleva-do el título de Psicología en lugar delde Ideología , él no se hubiera dado á conocer del público . Finalmente , le acon-sejamos con la franqueza que nos es característica , que re-cobre la calma , lea con interés y detenimiento el artículo que ha querido destruir , y si piensa sentar plaza de crítico aproveche sus sanas doctrinas y los principios luminosos que contiene , pues de esta suerte procederá siempre con exactitud y método , aprenderá á proponer       una cuestión li .

to think. The writer of the article says in the 7th paragraph of his public debut that “Psychology is the study of ideas,” and, expressing himself thus in so general and vague a manner, he must necessarily agree that for this study it is proper to begin with the origin of our ideas, of those that are acquired first, and to follow the gradual development of the other ideas, so as to have a complete and exact knowledge of them. These and no others are the rules prescribed by a true and luminous philosophy, and which he who devotes himself to the study of the sciences ought to follow. He who dispenses with this fundamental basis of later knowledge will stumble upon error at every step, will not know how to uphold the truth, and his writings will bear a stamp of clumsiness and inexactitude. Therefore the study of Ideology is necessary for that of Literature; therefore Mr. Systematist has proved nothing with his articles.

We shall conclude by observing that in the article “Ideology” nothing is said of sensationalism, nothing of spiritualism; that there is not in it so much as one idea, one opinion, from which the school to which its author belongs might be suspected. In writing it he sought to encourage the youth of our country so that, proceeding always in accordance with ideological principles, they might think with exactness and, making their productions worthy of the esteem and consideration of sensible men, might thus contribute to the advancement of the sciences and to the progress of enlightenment. We are persuaded that if this same article, which Mr. Systematist has criticized so bitterly, had borne the title of Psychology instead of that of Ideology, he would not have made himself known to the public. Finally, we advise him, with the frankness that is characteristic of us, to recover his calm, to read with interest and deliberation the article he has tried to destroy, and, if he means to set up as a critic, to profit by the sound doctrines and luminous principles it contains; for in this way he will always proceed with exactness and method, and will learn to propose a literary

[p. 356]

> teraria , á sostener debidamente su opinión , y se verá libre de que salga á probarle sus errores y extravíos Un amante de la verdad . * ** Sr. Ecléctico         (1). A Lover of Truth.

Mr. Eclectic (1).

Moved by the interest which the question raised by you against Mr. M. Costales has aroused in us, and desiring to illustrate the matter with some observations, we earnestly beg you to answer the following questions, for we wish to know your way of thinking before giving our own opinion:

1st What you understand by idea and by abstraction, and whether you admit a difference between these two words.

2nd Whether the true philosopher ought or ought not to study the origin of our ideas.

3rd In the event of answering the preceding question in the affirmative, whether or not you admit that these are acquired through the senses.

4th If you deny that our first ideas have sensations for their cause, explain, in accordance with the philosophical doctrines you profess, why deaf-mutes from birth are so limited in their intellectual faculties.

5th Whether the ideas of justice, of goodness, etc. are innate, or the result of comparisons after man has exercised his senses; and whether these ideas can be had without some object being represented to our soul.

6th Ideas being a result of the exercise of the intellectual faculties, whether this exercise can take place without the intermediary of the brain and of the nerves, and whether our soul proceeds in isolation in the operations of thought.

7th If you answer the preceding question in the negative, explain, so far as it bears

(1) Diario de la Habana of September 27, 1838 (A. Z.).

[p. 357]

> ga relación con la filosofia , y conforme á las doctrinas que sigue , las causas de la locura y del idiotismo , diciéndonos al mismo tiempo si los idiotas tienen idea de Dios , de justi-cia, de bondad , de causa etc. y demás ideas abstractas cu-yo orígen parece quiere negar absolutamente á los sen-tidos . Deseamos con ansia la contestación á estas preguntas , y creemos al propio tiempo que V. Sr. Ecléctico no nos desai-rará , ( 1) pues así lo esperamos de los buenos deseos que manifiesta por los progresos de la ilustración . Con esta confianza soy de V. S. S. Q. B. S. M. El amigo de la juventud . ( 1) El Ecléctico no dió pública respuesta á estas preguntas y la po-lémica quedó abandonada (A. Z) .

on philosophy, and in conformity with the doctrines you follow, the causes of madness and of idiocy, telling us at the same time whether idiots have an idea of God, of justice, of goodness, of cause, etc., and the other abstract ideas whose origin you seem to wish to deny absolutely to the senses.

We eagerly await the answer to these questions, and we believe at the same time that you, Mr. Eclectic, will not slight us, (1) for so we hope from the good wishes you show for the progress of enlightenment. In this confidence I remain your faithful servant, who kisses your hand.

Political and Military Government OF HAVANA.

## VIII

## ROYAL ACADEMY OF BELLES-LETTRES OF BARCELONA

Et Rege et Lege. [By King and by Law]

I, the undersigned, Secretary of the R oyal A cademy of B elles -L ettres of B arcelona , certify that at the Meeting held on the twenty-ninth day of January of this year, Don José de la Luz Caballero was admitted as Corresponding Member, and in witness whereof, and that it may serve him as Title, I issue the present, which I sign in Barcelona on the tenth of March of one thousand eight hundred and forty-one.—Seen and approved.—Joaquín Rey.—President.—Ramón Muns.—Member Secretary.

IX.

—Mr. Turnbull held in Havana the offices of Consul of H. B. M. and Superintendent of liberated Africans, the latter created by virtue of the treaties concluded by the governments of Spain and England in the years 1817 and 1835, with the aim of effectively and really abolishing the traffic in African slaves. The English agent carried out his charge with tenacity, was always on the alert, and besieged with his remonstrances the Captain General, who at that time was Don Jerónimo Valdés.

The English Consul was far too great an obstacle for so many men interested in the continuance of the slave trade and in the treaties with England remaining a dead letter; and so it is understandable that General Valdés should have concluded the dispatch in which he reported to the government of the Metropolis the insubordination...... of a handful of Black laborers......, and however persuaded he was “that this incident was entirely isolated,” by stating the “urgent necessity” of driving the British Consul from the island. Turnbull was, then, the object of hatred in that unhappy society, and

[p. 365]

> pesadilla del general Valdés , á extremo de exclamar un día de 1842 la primera Autoridad de la Isla , en presencia de al- -gunas personas de su corte :     " Quién me quitara de enci-ma á este hombre !" El deseo de agradar al sátrapa fué el origen de la pretensión    de excluirle , inmediatamente que fué relevado , de la Sociedad Económica , que le contaba des-de 1838 en el número de sus socios corresponsales . ( José de la Luz Caballero . Estudio crítico por Manuel Sanguily . -Habana 1890. ) Χ. Instructiva del abogado D. José de la Luz Caballero.- ( Septiembre 26 de 1844. ) -Preguntado , si sabe ó presume cual sea la causa de hallarse guardando arresto en la actua-lidad . Contestó , que por habérsele intimado la órden de prisión del Excmo . Sr. Capitán General , por conducto del Sr. Sargento Mayor de la Plaza , por complicidad que le resul-taba en la causa de conspiración de negros en esta Isla . P. , si en ésta capital ú otro punto había conocido y tra-tado á Mr. David Turnbull , Cónsul que fué de S. M. B. en esta Isla , espresando en tal caso qué relaciones tuvo con él y cuando fué la última ocasión que le vió.-C. , que habrá cosa de cinco años le fué presentado en calidad de viajero instruído , en una corta mansión que hizo en esta Isla , antes de ser Cónsul y aún de haber publicado su obra sobre este país ; habiendo tenido con él todas las atenciones que se tienen con un extranjero en tales casos . Volvió después Turnbull á la Isla en calidad de Cónsul , y entónces fué este á visitar al declarante quien le pagó la visita , y aquí con-cluyó todo : que las ocupaciones por un lado y los males por otro ( hace cerca de cuatro años) le hicieron desapare-cer completamente de la escena del mundo . P. , si podía determinar cuántas ocasiones y en qué fecha visitó á Turnbull después que tomó posesión de su consu-lado.-C. , que sólo la vez á que se ha contraído en su an-terior respuesta , fué cuando únicamente estuvo en su casa, no teniendo presente la fecha , aunque es fácil averiguarla porque fué recien llegado aquel funcionario á esta capital en calidad de cónsul .

the nightmare of General Valdés, to the point that one day in 1842 the first Authority of the Island exclaimed, in the presence of some persons of his court: “Who will rid me of this man!”—The wish to please the satrap was the origin of the attempt to exclude him, immediately after he was relieved, from the Economic Society, which had counted him since 1838 among its corresponding members.—(José de la Luz Caballero. Estudio crítico, by Manuel Sanguily.—Havana 1890.)

X.

Preliminary statement of the lawyer Don José de la Luz Caballero.— (September 26, 1844.)—Asked whether he knows or presumes what is the cause of his being at present held under arrest.—He answered that it is because the order of imprisonment of His Excellency the Captain General was served on him, through the Town Major of the Fortress, for complicity resulting against him in the case of the conspiracy of Blacks in this Island.

P., whether in this capital or in some other place he had known and had dealings with Mr. David Turnbull, formerly Consul of H. B. M. in this Island, stating in that case what relations he had with him and when was the last occasion he saw him.—C., that some five years ago he was introduced to him in the character of a learned traveler, during a short stay he made in this Island, before he was Consul and even before he had published his work on this country; and that he showed him all the attentions that are shown to a foreigner in such cases. Turnbull afterwards returned to the Island in the character of Consul, and then he came to visit the declarant, who returned the visit, and there it all ended: for his occupations on the one hand and his ailments on the other (for nearly four years now) have made him disappear completely from the stage of the world.

P., whether he could state on how many occasions and on what date he visited Turnbull after the latter took possession of his consulate.—C., that the one time referred to in his previous answer was the only occasion on which he was in his house, not having the date in mind, though it is easy to ascertain, because that functionary had only just arrived in this capital in the character of consul.

[p. 366]

> - P. , en qué sociedad y por quién fué presentado la prime ra ocasión á Turnbull . C. , que en casa del Dr. Madden , médico de profesión , é individuo de la Comisión Mixta amigo suyo . P. , si recordaba los motivos sobre que giró la conversa-ción.-C. , que la conversación fué miscelánea , como suele ser en toda mesa , recordando que se habló mucho , entre otras cosas científicas , de Meteorología , señalando las dife-rencias entre los fenómenos tropicales y los de los climas europeos , habiendo hablado todos indistintamente sobre la materia . P. , quienes eran las demás personas presentes      - . formaban parte de la sociedad la familia del citado Madden C. , que y otros extranjeros del comercio , cuyos nombres no recuer-da , hallándose también varias señoras extranjeras , entre ellas la esposa del referido Madden . - P. , donde vivía entónces Mr. Turnbull. C. , que en la Calzada de San Luis Gonzaga , donde es público y notorio que vivió dicho sujeto . - . P. , si fue sólo á aquella visita   C. , que fué solo y le en-contró acompañado de su esposa , la cual le hizo el cumpli-do , por hallarse él á la sazón en las piezas interiores , y sin que durante aquel acto compareciese otra persona . - P. , sobre los particulares de la conversación . C. , que la visita fué breve y versó la conversación sobre particulares indiferentes y usuales en semejantes casos . P - , si tuvo relaciones de amistad con el Secretario de Turnbull . C. , que jamás . P. , sipor casualidad habló alguna ocasión con Mr. Turn-bull respecto al proyecto de emancipación absoluta de la esclavitud de esta Isla.-C. , que nunca . P. , si sabe ó ha llegado á presumir que Turnbull hubiese tratado de promover especies que tuviesen por objeto ex-citar la esclavitud , para que obtuviese su absoluta emanci-pación  -C    . , que ha oído decir lo que generalmente se ha contado sobre el particular . P. , si recuerda haber visitado ó frecuentado alguna So- -ciedad cerca del Convento de Paula , á la que concurriese una que otra vez Mr. Turnbull . C. , que es la primera noti-cia que tiene de semejante Sociedad . P. , si no tiene presente haber concurrido nuevamente á la casa de Mr. Turnbull en la época del gobierno del Exce-lentísimo Sr. D. Gerónimo Valdés , y en tal concepto si lo

P., in what company and by whom he was introduced to Turnbull the first time.—C., that at the house of Dr. Madden, a physician by profession and a member of the Mixed Commission, a friend of his.

P., whether he remembered the subjects on which the conversation turned.—C., that the conversation was miscellaneous, as it usually is at any table, and he remembers that there was much talk, among other scientific matters, of Meteorology, the differences between tropical phenomena and those of European climates being pointed out, all present having spoken indiscriminately on the subject.

P., who the other persons present were.—C., that the company was made up of the family of the said Madden and other foreigners engaged in commerce, whose names he does not remember, there being present also several foreign ladies, among them the wife of the aforesaid Madden.

P., where Mr. Turnbull then lived.—C., that on the Calzada de San Luis Gonzaga, where it is public and notorious that the said person lived.

P., whether he went alone on that visit.—C., that he went alone and found him accompanied by his wife, who did him the honors, he being at the time in the inner rooms, and without any other person appearing during that call.

P., as to the particulars of the conversation.—C., that the visit was brief and the conversation turned on indifferent matters, usual in such cases.

P., whether he had relations of friendship with Turnbull’s Secretary.—C., that never.

P., whether by chance he spoke at any time with Mr. Turnbull concerning the project for the absolute emancipation of the slaves of this Island.— C., that never.

P., whether he knows or has come to presume that Turnbull had attempted to spread notions intended to stir up the slaves, so that they might obtain their absolute emancipation.—C., that he has heard said what has been generally related on the matter.

P., whether he remembers having visited or frequented some Society near the Convent of Paula, which Mr. Turnbull attended now and then.— C., that this is the first news he has of any such Society.

P., whether he does not remember having gone again to Mr. Turnbull’s house in the period of the government of His Excellency Don Gerónimo Valdés, and in that case whether he

[p. 367]

> OBRAS DE DON JOSÉ DE LA LUZ .             367 -. verificó acompañado de un joven inglés , expresando así mismo el objeto . C , que nunca , ni solo ni acompañado , durante el tiempo a que se contrae la pregunta . - P. , si tampoco tiene presente haber hecho alguna entre-ga de dinero á Mr. Turnbull , y con qué objeto . C. , que ja-más en su vida ni á Mr. Turnbull ni a nadie de este mundo , ha entregado cantidades de dinero . P. , si tiene presente haber conferenciado con alguna per-sona acerca de la posición ventajosa en que se halla el cas-tillo Número 4.-C. , que jamás ha hablado de castillos . P. , si ha conocido en esta capital al pardo extranjero lla-mado Luis Gigaut . -C     , que en estos días , á su regreso de Francia , es la primera vez que lo ha oido nombrar . P. , si durante el gobierno del Excmo . Sr. D. Gerónimo Val-dés ha llevado relaciones íntimas de amistad con el Dr. don Santiago Bombalier , Ldo . D. Manuel Martinez Serrano , don Domingo del Monte , D. Juan de Dios Corona y demás indi-víduos que se nombran en esta actuación , que para la debi-da inteligencia del declarante se le indican por el Fiscal.- C. , que conoce al Dr. Bombalier ; que por muchos años ha llevado relaciones de amistad con los Ldos . Manuel Marti-nez Serrano y D. Domingo del Monte , y que respecto á las demás personas iudicadas , unas conoce y otras no , sin con-traerse á épocas determinadas ; pero de seguro no ha esta-do en contacto con ellas durante el gobierno del Sr. Valdés . P. , si con anterioridad habló el declarante con el Ldo . don Domingo del Monte y demás indivíduos que se le han indi-cado , sobre particulares relativos al proyecto de emancipa-ción absoluta de la esclavitud en esta Isla.-C. , que nunca . P. , si ha llegado á su conocimiento que algunas personas notables del país hayan influído de acuerdo con Mr. David - Turnbull , para que se llevase á efecto el referido plan de emancipación y en qué términos . C. , que jamás . P. , si ha llegado á su noticia que ciertas personas mez- -cladas en el indicado proyecto hayan influído fuera del país para su realización . C. que jamás . P. , si tampoco haya podido comprender el objeto y fin que hayan tenido ciertos movimientos que se advirtieron en las fincas del campo á fines del año próximo anterior y -C principio del actual .      , que hallándose en Europa ála sa-zón no puede determinar el objeto y fin de tales movimien-tos : allí llegaron las primeras noticias como alzamientos parciales de algunas fincas , y por consiguiente de todos

made it accompanied by a young Englishman, stating likewise the object. —C., that never, neither alone nor accompanied, during the time to which the question is confined.

P., whether he likewise does not remember having made some delivery of money to Mr. Turnbull, and for what object.—C., that never in his life has he handed over sums of money, either to Mr. Turnbull or to anyone else in this world.

P., whether he has conferred with any person concerning the advantageous position in which the castle Number 4 stands.—C., that he has never spoken of castles.

P., whether he has known in this capital the foreign mulatto named Luis Gigaut.—C., that these days, on his return from France, are the first time he has heard him named.

P., whether during the government of His Excellency Don Gerónimo Valdés he has maintained intimate relations of friendship with Dr. Don Santiago Bombalier, Lic. Don Manuel Martínez Serrano, Don Domingo del Monte, Don Juan de Dios Corona and the other individuals named in these proceedings, who are pointed out to him by the Prosecutor for the declarant’s proper understanding.—C., that he knows Dr. Bombalier; that for many years he has had relations of friendship with the Licentiates Manuel Martínez Serrano and Don Domingo del Monte, and that as regards the other persons indicated, he knows some and not others, without restricting this to particular periods; but that he has certainly not been in contact with them during the government of Mr. Valdés.

P., whether at an earlier time the declarant spoke with Lic. Don Domingo del Monte and the other individuals who have been pointed out to him about particulars relating to the project for the absolute emancipation of the slaves in this Island.—C., that never.

P., whether it has come to his knowledge that some notable persons of the country have worked, in concert with Mr. David Turnbull, to have the said plan of emancipation carried into effect, and on what terms.—C., that never.

P., whether it has come to his notice that certain persons mixed up in the said project have worked from outside the country for its realization.— C. that never.

P., whether he has likewise been unable to understand the object and purpose of certain movements that were observed on the country estates toward the end of the year just past and the beginning of the present one. —C., that, being in Europe at the time, he cannot determine the object and purpose of such movements: there the first news of them arrived as partial uprisings on some estates, and consequently of all

[p. 368]

> fueron calificados como las demás sublevaciones negreras , que de cuando en cuando han estallado en la Isla ; después fué cuando los periódicos comenzaron á hablar de una conspiración más general , con ramificaciones en varios puntos de la Isla , que se decía descubierta por el Go-bieruo . P. , si no tiene algún dato para presumir que en esos mo-vimientos hayan influído poderosamente ciertas personas interesadas por sus fines y principios , ansiosas acaso de obtener por semejantes medios innovaciones respecto al sis-tema de gobierno que rige en esta Isla.-C. , que ni tiene , ni cree que puedan existir semejantes datos . P. , en qué fecha se ausentó el declarante de esta capital y á que punto se dirigió , es decir , la última vez que lo veri-ficó.-C. , que el 29 de Mayo de 1843 partió de la Habana para New- York , donde se embarcó al cabo de quince días para Havre de Gracia , á cuyo punto llegó el 20 de Julio , y por fin á París el 24 del mismo , habiendo residido constan-temente en esa Capital hasta su regreso en 15 de Agosto próximo pasado . - P. , si puede manifestar el objeto de ese viaje . C. , que su objeto es de pública notoriedad    y aconsejado además por facultativos de nota : el restablecimiento de su salud , como consta al mismo gobierno de la Isla . P. , con que persona de esta Capital ó de otros puntos de la Isla ha llevado correspondencia durante su ausencia.- C. , que con ninguna , por su casi imposibilidad de escribir sin gran detrimento de su salud , como consta á la Isla en-tera ; no habiendo escrito más que algunas esquelas á su consorte , que más bien pueden llamerse partes de salud lo que pueden certificar igualmente cuantos le vieron en París y sobre todo los primeros médicos de dicha Capital . - P. , si durante su asiento en París tuvo alguna entrevista con el Ldo . D. Domingo del Monte . C. , que lo veía fami-liar y frecuentemente ( pues no ha tenido motivos para lo contrario ) como sucede entre amigos y paisanos . P. , si en alguna de sus conversaciones el Ldo . D. Domin-go del Monte le habló sobre Mr. David Turnbull y de los proyectos que este tenía entre manos para que se llevase á efecto la emancipación de la esclavitud en ésta.-C. , que nunca . - P. , si absolutamente recuerda haber tratado de esos par-ticulares con ninguna persona  .   C. , que con nadie .

of them, they were classed like the other Black uprisings that have broken out from time to time in the Island; it was afterwards that the newspapers began to speak of a more general conspiracy, with ramifications in various parts of the Island, which was said to have been discovered by the Government.

P., whether he has no evidence for presuming that those movements were powerfully influenced by certain persons, interested on account of their aims and principles, eager perhaps to obtain by such means innovations in the system of government that rules in this Island.—C., that he neither has, nor believes there can exist, any such evidence.

P., on what date the declarant absented himself from this capital and to what place he went, that is, the last time he did so.—C., that on the 29th of May of 1843 he left Havana for New York, where at the end of fifteen days he embarked for Havre de Grâce, at which place he arrived on the 20th of July, and finally at Paris on the 24th of the same month, having resided constantly in that Capital until his return on the 15th of August last.

P., whether he can state the object of that journey.—C., that its object is a matter of public notoriety, and was besides advised by physicians of note: the restoration of his health, as is known to the very government of the Island.

P., with what person of this Capital or of other parts of the Island he has kept up a correspondence during his absence.—C., that with none, owing to his near impossibility of writing without great detriment to his health, as the whole Island knows; having written nothing but a few notes to his wife, which may rather be called bulletins of his health, as can likewise be certified by all who saw him in Paris, and above all by the first physicians of that Capital.

P., whether during his stay in Paris he had any interview with Lic. Don Domingo del Monte.—C., that he saw him familiarly and frequently (for he has had no reasons for doing otherwise), as happens between friends and countrymen.

P., whether in any of their conversations Lic. Don Domingo del Monte spoke to him about Mr. David Turnbull and the projects he had in hand for carrying into effect the emancipation of the slaves in this Island.—C., that never.

P., whether he remembers at all having treated of those particulars with any person whatever.—C., that with no one.

[p. 369]

> P. , si no tiene presente haber oido decir que tanto don Domingo del Monte como otras personas hayan trabajado -eficazmente de acuerdo con Mr. Turnbull para que se lle-vase á cabo la espresada emancipación . C. , que ha oldo hablar generalmente y hasta con indignación sobre el par-ticular , como una imputación que se le hacía en esta causa ; teniéndola todos por una solemne impostura . P. , si el declarante juzga libre de responsabilidad al se-ñor del Monte en la presente causa , y que fundamento tie-ne para ello.-C. , que la pregunta no está bien hilada , y por tanto se abstiene de contestarla . El Fiscal manifestó al declarante que su objeto al hacer-le la anterior pregunta se contraía á que consignase su opinión respecto á los sentimientos del Sr. del Monte en ia cuestión de emancipación y que al mismo tiempo es-presase si le consideraba capaz de haber influído en los acontecimientos que á fines del año anterior se advirtieron en la jurisdicción de Matanzas y Cárdenas ; pues habiendo -llevado estrechas relaciones con dicho sujeto muy bien pu-diera emitir su opinión sobre el particular . C. , que en pri-mer lugar la prueba de que la anterior pregunta no estaba bien concebida , y que ni aún espresaba la idea del Sr. Fis-cal , es la explanación que acaba de dar , como será fácil de-mostrarlo en otra oportunidad , no haciéndolo ahora por evitar proligidad ; y contrayéndose á la pregunta responde , que siempre le ha oido hablar en sentido contrario á la emancipación , considerándole incapaz no ya de influir, pero ni aún de concebir la idea de semejantes acontecimientos , pues en todas sus relaciones con el Ldo . D. Domingo del Monte le ha encontrado siempre amante decidido del país , y como tal se honra con su amistad el exponente . P. , si ha llegado á concebir la idea de que el Cónsul que fué de S. M. B. en esta Isla , Mr. Turnbull , haya maquinado para la alteración del orden en la misma , propendiendo con entusiasmo al alzamiento de la esclavitud ; espresando á la vez el fundamento que haya tenido para ello.-C. , que así lo oyó decir cuando le pusieron preso , hallándose á la sazón enfermo el declarante fuera de la ciudad . P. , si llegó á su conocimiento que durante la época del Exmo . Sr. D. Jerónimo Valdés , varios miembros de la So-ciedad de Amigos del País , escandalizados de la conducta observada por Mr. Turnbull hubiesen hecho una moción pidiendo que su nombre se borrase de aquella Corporación 24

P., whether he does not remember having heard it said that Don Domingo del Monte as well as other persons have worked effectively in concert with Mr. Turnbull to bring about the said emancipation.—C., that he has heard it spoken of generally, and even with indignation, as an imputation that was being made against him in this case; everyone holding it to be a solemn imposture.

P., whether the declarant judges Mr. del Monte free of responsibility in the present case, and on what grounds.—C., that the question is not well put together, and he therefore abstains from answering it.

The Prosecutor explained to the declarant that his object in putting the foregoing question to him was confined to having him record his opinion as to the sentiments of Mr. del Monte on the question of emancipation, and at the same time state whether he considered him capable of having had an influence on the events that were observed toward the end of last year in the jurisdiction of Matanzas and Cárdenas; for, having kept up close relations with that person, he could very well give his opinion on the matter.—C., that in the first place the proof that the previous question was not well conceived, and did not even express the Prosecutor’s idea, is the explanation he has just given, as it will be easy to demonstrate on another occasion, which he does not do now to avoid prolixity; and confining himself to the question, he answers that he has always heard him speak in a sense contrary to emancipation, and considers him incapable not merely of exerting an influence on such events, but even of conceiving the idea of them; for in all his relations with Lic. Don Domingo del Monte he has always found him a decided lover of the country, and as such the deponent is honored by his friendship.

P., whether he has come to conceive the idea that the former Consul of H. B. M. in this Island, Mr. Turnbull, plotted to disturb the order in it, working with enthusiasm toward a rising of the slaves; stating at the same time the grounds he may have had for it.—C., that he heard it said so when they arrested him, the declarant being at the time ill outside the city.

P., whether it came to his knowledge that during the time of His Excellency Don Jerónimo Valdés, several members of the Society of Friends of the Country, scandalized by the conduct observed by Mr. Turnbull, had made a motion asking that his name be struck from the rolls of that respectable

[p. 370]

> respetable , considerando que era una anomalía que entre -los Amigos del País fuese contado como socio corresponsal el que bajo todos aspectos procuraba destruirlo . C. , que es menester distinguir épocas, pues la moción se hizo mu-cho tiempo antes de haber sido preso Turnbull y cuando estaba poco antes en el pleno ejercicio de sus funciones con-sulares , y como tal en correspondencia y demás relaciones con el Gobierno de la Isla ; y contrayéndose á la cuestión misma , en el seno de la Sociedad , se refiere el declarante en todas sus partes al oficio que como Director de dicha Corporación pasó en aquellas circunstancias . P - .. si dicha moción se hizo antes ó después de haber sido preso Mr. Turnbull . C . , que queda contestado en su ante-rior respuesta , P. , si era Director de la Sociedad Económica cuando aconteció la prisión de Mr. Turnbull , y qué temperamento -tomó aquel cuerpo respetable en vista de dicha circuns-tancia . C. , que crée era Director en aquella época , pues lo fué desde fines de 1842 ; y que ignora que la Sociedad to-mase medida alguna con motivo de la referida circuns-tancia . - P. , de qué sentido fué el declarante con respecto á la moción á que aluden las anteriores contestaciones . C ., que su referido oficio no deja que desear en la materia . P. , si real y efectivamente el declarante ignoraba en la época -de la moción , que Mr. Turnbull se hacía remarcable por su exaltacion en orden á la cuestión de emancipación . C. , que había oido hablar mucho de sus reclamaciones reiteradas como órgano del Gobierno Británico para la cesación de la trata , y de algunos pasos que daba en dcsempeño de su mi-nisterio en calidad de Super - Intendente de los emancipados (pues reunía ambos cargos ) admitido como tal por el Go-bierno Supremo y por el de esta Isla . P. , si llegó á comprender el objeto que tuvo Mr. David Turnbull para desembarcar furtivamente en las playas de esta Isla , y por cuya razón se le redujo á prisión . C. , que ignora el motivo porque lo hiciera furtivamente . P. , si tampoco pudo comprender el fin político que se propusiese Mr. Turnbull , para introducirse de aquella suer-te en esta Isla.-C. , que nada le consta en cuanto al fin político ; y que lo único que oyó decir generalmente en aquella época fué que había venido á reclamar cierto número de negros de no sabe que colonia extrangera que

Corporation, considering it an anomaly that among the Friends of the Country there should be counted as a corresponding member one who in every respect was trying to destroy it.—C., that it is necessary to distinguish periods, for the motion was made a long time before Turnbull was arrested, and when shortly before he had been in the full exercise of his consular functions, and as such in correspondence and other relations with the Government of the Island; and confining himself to the question itself, within the Society, the declarant refers in all its parts to the official letter which, as Director of that Corporation, he sent in those circumstances.

P., whether the said motion was made before or after Mr. Turnbull was arrested.—C., that this has been answered in his previous reply.

P., whether he was Director of the Economic Society when the arrest of Mr. Turnbull took place, and what course that respectable body took in view of that circumstance.—C., that he believes he was Director at that time, for he was so from the end of 1842; and that he does not know of the Society’s having taken any measure on account of the said circumstance.

P., of what mind the declarant was with respect to the motion to which the foregoing answers allude.—C., that his said official letter leaves nothing to be desired on the matter.

P., whether the declarant really and truly did not know, at the time of the motion, that Mr. Turnbull was making himself conspicuous by his zeal in the matter of the question of emancipation.—C., that he had heard much talk of his repeated remonstrances, as the organ of the British Government, for the cessation of the slave trade, and of some steps he was taking in the discharge of his ministry in the character of Superintendent of the emancipated (for he held both offices), admitted as such by the Supreme Government and by that of this Island.

P., whether he came to understand the object Mr. David Turnbull had in landing furtively on the shores of this Island, for which reason he was placed under arrest.—C., that he does not know the reason why he should have done so furtively.

P., whether he likewise could not understand the political end Mr. Turnbull may have had in view in introducing himself in that manner into this Island.—C., that he knows nothing as to the political end; and that the only thing he heard generally said at that time was that he had come to claim a certain number of Blacks, from he knows not what foreign colony, who

[p. 371]

> se hallaban como esclavos en uno ó varios ingenios de la Vuelta -Arriba , en desempeño de sus funciones de Super - In-tendente de emancipados africanos . P. , si le consta ó ha oido decir que durante el tiempo en que ejerció Mr. Turnbull el destino de Cónsul , se hubiesen introducido en esta Isla por su disposición , armas y otros pertrechos de guerra , y con que fin.-C. , que es la primera noticia que tiene sobre el particular . P. , si ha oido decir que algunas personas hayan contri- -buido con dinero ó de otra suerte para que se proporciona-sen dichas armas . C. , que tampoco le consta , y ni aún lo creería , si se le contara , de hijos del país . P. , si no infiere que en este país existe un partido que bajo todos aspectos ha tratado de acuerdo con Mr. David Turnbull , de levantar la esclavitud para obtener á la sombra -de las dificultades que necesariamente habría de encontrar el Gobierno , innovaciones en política    . . C , que crée que ni existe , ni puede existir, comprometiéndose á llevar la evi-dencia sobre la materia hasta á los ánimos más prevenidos . - P. , si con el actual Cónsul de S. M. B. ha llevado relacio-nes íntimas de amistad el declarante ó de otra suerte . C. , que ni de vista le conoce . P. , si ha oido decir ó le consta que este funcionario esté -identificado con las ideas de Mr. Turnbull tocante al proyec-to de emancipación . C ., que nada sabe sobre el particular . P. , si ha conocido en esta capital á D. Francisco Senma-nat , y qué clases de relaciones ha llevado con él.-C. , que le ha conocido de vista , y hace tantos años , que ni recuerda á punto fijo la última vez que lo vió . P. , si ha oido decir el objeto que tuvo este individuo para venir á este país á fines del año próximo anterior , C. , que ni lo sabe , ni puede graduarlo , porque se hallaba á la sazon á dos mil leguas de distancia . P. , si el declarante ha tenido parte en algún proyecto de -conspiración que haya tenido por objeto la emancipación absoluta de la esclavitud en esta Isla , expresando en tal caso el fin político que le animaba al efecto   .    C. , que el decla-rante en lo que ha tomado y tomará siempre parte es y será en restañar y cicatrizar las heridas que otras manos han inferido á su patria , por cuya ventura derramará hasta su última gota de sangre . - P. , quiénes son en su concepto los que han inferido esas heridas á su patria y de que medios se han valido . C. , que

were held as slaves on one or several sugar estates of the Vuelta-Arriba, in the discharge of his functions as Superintendent of emancipated Africans.

P., whether he knows or has heard it said that during the time Mr. Turnbull held the post of Consul, arms and other munitions of war were brought into this Island by his arrangement, and to what end.—C., that this is the first news he has on the matter.

P., whether he has heard it said that some persons contributed money or otherwise toward procuring the said arms.—C., that he knows nothing of that either, nor would he even believe it, if he were told it, of sons of the country.

P., whether he does not infer that there exists in this country a party which in every respect has tried, in concert with Mr. David Turnbull, to raise the slaves, in order to obtain, under cover of the difficulties the Government would necessarily encounter, innovations in politics.—C., that he believes it neither exists nor can exist, and pledges himself to carry evidence on the matter even to the most prejudiced minds.

P., whether the declarant has kept up relations of intimate friendship, or of any other kind, with the present Consul of H. B. M.—C., that he does not even know him by sight.

P., whether he has heard it said, or knows, that this functionary is identified with the ideas of Mr. Turnbull touching the project of emancipation. —C., that he knows nothing on the matter.

P., whether he has known in this capital Don Francisco Senmanat, and what kind of relations he has kept up with him.—C., that he has known him by sight, and so many years ago that he does not even remember exactly the last time he saw him.

P., whether he has heard what object this individual had in coming to this country at the end of last year.—C., that he neither knows it nor can gauge it, since he was at that time two thousand leagues away.

P., whether the declarant has had any part in some project of conspiracy that had as its object the absolute emancipation of the slaves in this Island, stating in that case the political end that moved him to it.—C., that what the declarant has taken and will always take part in is, and will be, staunching and healing the wounds that other hands have inflicted on his country, for whose welfare he will shed his blood to the last drop.

P., who in his view are those who have inflicted those wounds on his country, and what means they have used.—C., that

[p. 372]

> no es esta la oportunidad de manifestarlo , por ser necesa-rio entrar en un análisis circunstanciado que corresponde á otro lugar . P. , si sospecha que algunas personas llevadas de espíritu -de animadversión hacia el declarante , le hayan perjudicado en la presente causa directa ó indirectamente . C. , que así debe creerlo al ver lo que se practica con la inocencia . P. , si el declarante ha llevado relaciones de amistad con -algunos jefes de la República de Méjico y Costa - firme que hayan estado en esta capital . C    . , que jamás . P. , si ha llevado relaciones de amistad con D. Félix Ma-ría Tanco , y en tal caso si se ha reunido con él ú otra per-sona del mismo apellido , en alguna Sociedad en esta Capital , ó fuera de ella.-C. , que han sido pocas sus relaciones con D. Félix Tanco , pues este señor casi siempre ha residido en Matanzas donde era Administrador de Correos , conociéndo-se ambos de nombre , y habiendo hecho una visita al decla-rante en esta ciudad , cuando se hallaba enfermo á su regreso de los Estados Unidos . P. , si el declarante conoció al pardo Gabriel de la Concep-ción Valdés ( a) Plácido , é igualmente por algún motivo al moreno Miguel Flores . nocido nunca . -C      , que á ninguno de los dos ha co- P. , si ha oido decir que los antedichos Plácido y Flores hayan sido emisarios de Mr. Turnbull y de ciertas Socieda-des establecidas en esta Capital para que se llevara a efec-to el plan de emancipación.--- C. , que lo primero lo ignora , y lo segundo lo ignora y lo duda sobremanera . P. , si tampoco á oido decir que una de esas Sociedades -tuviese asiento en casa de D. José Ayala , la cual era com-puesta de personas blancas y de color . C. , que mal puede saber las circunstancias el que ignora la existencia . En este estado dispuso el Sr. Fiscal la suspensión del ac-to para continuarlo cuando fuese necesario en el curso del procedimiento , se le leyó al abogado declarante , expresó estar conforme , advirtiendo únicamente que en vista del tenor de ciertas preguntas que se le hacen en el presente interrogatorio , se vé forzado á establecer la más solemne protesta , para que obre sus efectos cuanto ha lugar en dere- -                  -cho llegado el caso de manifestar las irregularidades á que se contrae ......- Fernández Cotá . Pedro Salazar .    José de la Luz . José *

this is not the occasion to state it, for it would be necessary to enter upon a detailed analysis which belongs elsewhere.

P., whether he suspects that some persons, moved by a spirit of animosity toward the declarant, have injured him in the present case, directly or indirectly.—C., that he must believe so, on seeing how innocence is dealt with.

P., whether the declarant has kept up relations of friendship with any chiefs of the Republic of Mexico and of the Spanish Main who have been in this capital.—C., that never.

P., whether he has kept up relations of friendship with Don Félix María Tanco, and in that case whether he has met with him, or with another person of the same surname, in any Society in this Capital or outside it.—C., that his relations with Don Félix Tanco have been few, for this gentleman has almost always resided in Matanzas, where he was Postmaster, the two knowing each other by name, and he having paid the declarant a visit in this city when he was ill on his return from the United States.

P., whether the declarant knew the mulatto Gabriel de la Concepción Valdés, alias Plácido, and likewise, for any reason, the Black Miguel Flores. —C., that he has never known either of the two.

P., whether he has heard it said that the aforesaid Plácido and Flores were emissaries of Mr. Turnbull and of certain Societies established in this Capital for carrying the plan of emancipation into effect.—C., that the first he does not know, and the second he does not know and very much doubts.

P., whether he has likewise not heard it said that one of those Societies had its seat in the house of Don José Ayala, and was composed of white persons and persons of color.—C., that he who does not know of its existence can hardly know its circumstances.

At this point the Prosecutor ordered the proceeding suspended, to be continued when necessary in the course of the trial; it was read to the deponent lawyer, who declared himself in agreement, observing only that, in view of the tenor of certain questions put to him in the present interrogatory, he finds himself obliged to enter the most solemn protest, that it may have all the effects allowed by law when the time comes to set forth the irregularities to which he refers......—Pedro Salazar.—José de la Luz.—José Fernández Cotá.
